div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By IdARjORIE.

Royal Palaces as Hospitals. Balmoral is being converted into a hospital for naval and military officers recuperating from their wounds. Other houses on the estates are to be used as base hospitals for the troops, notably Abergeldie and Birkhall. Barton Manor is another of the King's houses in which convalescent officers will be received. A bachelor's wing has been added to York Cottage, which will in future be reserved for the use of Their Majesties' two elder sons when shooting at Sandringham. Here the Princes will live and receive their friends, as the Cottage is not large enough to accommodate the King's Family now that the elder members are growing up.

Martial London. London has in the last three months taken on an unaccustomed martial air, and is fast be- coming a military city. Men in khaki are to be seen in great numbers in all the streets. The one-time quiet gardens of the Temple resound to the word of command, as the assembled re- cruits go through i their daily drill. Grey motors swiftly convey staff officers from point to point, the now 1' miliar O.H.M.S. standing out on the wind-scr- nof the cars. Shop fronts are in some cases r: Imost entirely given over to war outfits and Red Cross requisites, and last, but not least, the darkened trams and onani- buses, and the barely half-lighted streets, bring home to everyone the gloom of the war-cloud that has changed not only our lives, but the appearance of our city streets, parks, and squares.

div.head: GERMAN IRON TRADE. Canada to Benefit by Enemy's Loss.
div.p: GERMAN IRON TRADE. Canada to Benefit by Enemy's Loss.

Mr. H. Whitham, San Francisco, who has recently visited Canada, sends us the following cutting from a Canadian paper : Shut off from Britain by a steel wall, Ger- many is to lose to Canada and the United States one of the biggest and most lucrative of her ex- port markets, viz., unfinished iron and steel pro- ' ducts. ' • - •

To replace. the huge German output of wire nails, wire rods, steam tubes, bars and sheet metal, a syndicate of British manufacturers is sending over to Canada a special commissioner, P. G. Donald, who will make arrangements with the steel mills of Canada for the supplying of the world's biggest steel market. Great Britain in the first six months of this year imported from Germany 28,000 tons of wire nails. Her imports of telegraph wire in the same period totalled 14,000 tons, steam tubes 24,000 tons, bars, angles and shapes 215,000 tons. Germany, the world's second largest producer of pig iron, had, by reason of her close proximity, the bulk of this huge market for raw and unfin- ished steel and iron products. To take Germany's place in supplying the great finishing plants of Britain with practically every line of wire and steel goods, will tax the capacity of every steel and iron mill in Canada and the United States. For some months the steel trade in Canada has been dull, and the present conditions will nd the Canadian manufacturer quite ready to esert himself to the utmost to obtain and hold this lucrative business.

white clear muslin, or touches of Paisley silk. Some have double skirts. They are made in colours also, and are especially attractive in saxe-blue, grey, mole, and many shades of brown. Equally desirable are the black taffetas, ready-to-wear gowns, with pleated tunics, hand- some sashes, and touches of Russian and Orien- tal embroideries. The materials used for this class of garment are remarkable for their excellent quality and beautiful colouring. Pinafores and Walking Dresses. Another style of dress that should commend itself to the frugal Ininded is the new pinafore which affords a great deal of variety for a very small outlay. Sleeveless, with large armholes, and buttoning down the front, it is quickly and easily slipped over different blouses and dresses, and at once transforms them, even when of ancient make, into fashionable and pretty toilettes. These pinafores have the godet hip, which consists of an inverted pleat at each side —one mode of increasing the width of winter skirts. The walking-dress, made to wear with- out a coat, is very much in evidence, probably because the mild weather admits of lighter gar- ments just now. It generally consists of a coat-like tunic and narrow underskirt. The former is bordered with fur, or one of the many substitutes. Imitation astrakan is very suitable and is used for the close fitting collars and cuffs. A Cossack cap of the same completes the costume.

• Autumn Blouses. Blouses show no sign of going out of favour, and, like the sports coat, improve with time. Brocaded crepes, soft satins, both dull and bright in surface, and broche silks, are all favourite materials for blouses and shirts. A very transparent canvas-like fabric, soft and supple, intended for wearing over coloured slips, is among the novelties, and is at its best in tan and wool shades. This season's blouses are distinguished for their simplicity, and there is no elaborate trimming, or exaggerated adorn- ment, yet all are smart, and beautiful in col- ouring. One model in dull navy broche silk had the quaintest of double collars, made of clear muslin. In fact, all the newest designs are finished with collars, cuffs, and guirapes of this fresh, dainty material. The waistcoat makes a variety and in some instances is crossed at the waist, where it forms a sash, the ends being trimmed with fringe.

div.head: HINTS ON • HEALTH. Useful Information in Popular Language.
div.p: HINTS ON • HEALTH. Useful Information in Popular Language.

The Need for Good Mothercraft. The great majority of infants who fail to survive the crisis of the first year, die, not because they are starved, or ovetcrowded, or underclothed, or neglected, although naturally these factors have an influence; but chiefly be- cause they are fed too generously, too often, and improperly; because they are strangled in too many clothes and asphyxiated from want of air; and because they are nursed, and com- forted, and cuddled too much; they die, in fact, from want of good mothercraL, and not from neglect or unavoidable causes associated with our economic system.—Dr. Eric Pritchard in the "Contemporary Review" for November. Chilblain Troubles. - -

- -----._... The weather is not cold enough yet for chil- blains to present themselves, but a is not too early to take a few precautions, and perhaps prevent them from appearing at all, and this can be done by wearing woollen or silk stock- ings, and occasionally rubbing warm olive oil into the feet. Plenty of exercise to promote circulation is also a good preventive. For the benefit of those who always suffer when the cold weather comes, I recommend the following: loz. tincture of eantharides, Oz. soap liniment, ioz. spirits of camphor. Mix well and apply when the trouble first appears. Camphorated oil is excellent to use for young children, and ,should be warmed before use. Four drachms spirits of turpentine and 8 drachms camphor- ated, oil well mixed together is anothrr very good remedy. ' If the feet are kept cramped up in boots or shoes which do not fit comfortably, chilblains and all kinds of discomforts must result. It is as important to bestow as much care on the feet as upon the face or hands: Well wash the feet every night in hot water, and if the chilblains have not yet appeared, rub in warm olive oil. Very tender feet should never be washed without powdering afterwards. —"M." in " Farm and Home."

NOVEMBER FIFTH, 1914. (BY JESSIE Sum.) "The world seems glad to-night, boys, Come, gather round the fire; We'll set old Fawkes alight, boys, Upon a tarry pyre! He'll make a famous blaze, boys; A sight 'twill be to see. So gather round and gaze, boys, . In goodly company !".

Yet all is sad to-night, boys, For greater fires must burn 'Ere Right shall vanquish Might, boys. Hearts still must hopeless yearn For Motherland and home, boys: For those beneath the sod, Who shed their precious life's blood To win the cause of God.

div.head: MORE POTATO AVART. Farmer Fined at the County Sessions.
div.p: MORE POTATO AVART. Farmer Fined at the County Sessions.

At the County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Vice-Chancellor Stewart Smith, and Messrs. It. C. Parr, W. Furness and H. P. Mortimer, Robert Hunter, farmer, of Ashton- in-Makerfield, was fined 40s. and costs for fail- ing to notify the existence of wart disease amongst his potato crop.—He pleaded guilty. Mr. S. J. F. Loe, sub-inspector, of the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, said that he visited defendant's farm on September 17th, after receiving information that defendant had been sending diseased potatoes to the Warring- ton Market. Defendant admitted that he had seen the growth on the tops of the potatoes. A notice stating that the disease was a notifi- able one had been served upon him. Inspector Snell, of the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, spoke of the risk of the disease spreading to other farms if it was allowed to pass unnoticed in any one .place. The Inspector, in answer to a question by the. Chairman, said that there was no difficulty in deteding the diseased potatoes before they were dug up, for there was a superficial growth, which showed on the tops of the plant. There were about thirty varieties of potatoes which were immune from the disease, and all the Board asked was that farmers should plant one or other of those varieties in the affected fields. Defendant said he had done his best. He got fresh seed from Scotland every year and he also limed the field. It was only a vei'y slight case. . .
At the conclusion of the Court's business, Inspector Snell made a formal application on behalf of ILM. Treasury for half of the fine. This was granted.

div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.

increased a hundred-fold, and it seems that a Dutch grower of bulbs is converting his pro- duce into flour. Holland exports vast quantities of bulbs, and has huge stores in the country; consequently the discovery may prove impor- tant The flour from the bulbs is mixed with that of wheat, barley and rye, and the results are said to be very satisfactory. The Germans, rumour says, are using large quantities of the 'flour. The lily, leek, and onion belong to the bulb family; strangely enough, the narcissus only is poisonous, therefore not edible.

Women as Administrators. We have lady mayors and town councillors, and recently there was a sensible departure from established custom by the appointment of a woman master of the Workhouse at Baintree, Essex, where the number of inmates is seldom less than two hundred. The " master "is matron also, and she has a woman assistant. When it is considered that thousands of women are confined in public, .as well as private lunatic asylums, it is astonishing that no effort is made to compel the Government to appoint women commissioners and doctors in these often doubt- fully conducted institutions. That the lives of so many women should be under the abso- lute control and direction of Men commissioners, and men doctors only, is probably due to the fact that the sane are generally indifferent to the conditions of life they impose upon the insane. Also being segregated, helpless, and often friendless, the latter cannot make their disabilities and disadvantages known to the out- side world. Women could do much to help the unfortunate insane if they took this matter up. as vigorously as they have fought industrial and economic abuses. There is a wide field for women's activities in the study and practice of mental diseases.

Inexpensive Ready-to-Wear Frocks. To buy wisely and carefully is a duty this year; not to buy at all, except where a stern necessity forbids the smallest outlay, is to bring hardship on hundreds of women workers. To those who are seeking smart and inexpensive gowns the ready-to-wear frocks shown this winter are marvels of good taste, cut and finish, and, at the same time, most moderate in price. The new models in black velveteen, for after- noon wear, are simplicity itself, and charm- ingly relieved with collars and guimpes of

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
FARMERS AND THE WAR OFFICE. A Lancashire Grievance.

The question of the supply of farm produce to the Army was discussed at length at a meet- ing of the Council of the Lancashire Farmers' Association held at Preston on Saturday. Mr. Fitzherbert (Brockholes) said many Lan- cashire farmers, in dealing with the War Office authorities, had found that the great stumbling block was that. though the samples. and •price of the commodities might be agreed upon the transaction had to be dealt with by other offi- cers, and the produce might be thrown back upon the hands of the farmers. If any good had to be done the purchas4 ought to be settled and ratified at the same time it was effected, and no other person should have the power to reject it. The hope was expressed that the new County Committee would be able to facilitate and regu- larise the direct purchase from farmers; and a resolution was approved pressing for arrange- ments between County Committees and the War Office under which any purchase of pro- duce at the farm should not be subject to sub- sequent rejection after delivery.

div.head: HOME SUGAR INDUSTRY.
div.p: HOME SUGAR INDUSTRY.

It is yet uncertain, says "Farm and Home," whether the important step taken by the Gov- ernment of prohibiting the importation of sugar from European countries inaugurates a change in the attitude hitherto taken towards the home production or is merely a move in the great game war which is at present being car- ried on before the eyes of a horrified world. Its immediate effect is no doubt to deprive Germany of an opportunity of raising money by the sale of the crop which it has reaped; but it is to be hoped that the movement will not stop here, and that the Government, having spent a huge sum to prevent a sugar famine in the land, will realise the desirability of encour- aging production at home, and do this by the direct and effective means of helping the sugar factory to gain a sound footing before it has to depend on its own resources. There are plenty of people with enterprise enough to take up a risky business if they can weigh all the pro- babilities beforehand, but in the case of sugar production, bounty-fed abroad and affected by the fantastic arbitrariness associated with the decision of political questions at home, the most far-seeing have to acknowledge that it is im- possible to forecast what may be the position of affairs a few years hence. A little nibney spent judiciously at the start, coupled with a settled policy regarding duties, would soon put a different complexion on the prospects of the home sugar industry; and now or never is the time to set about the work.

div.head: SUPPLIES OF POTASH.
div.p: SUPPLIES OF POTASH.

The war has stopped the importation from Germany of kaind and sulphate of potash, which we have got to look upon as being cm- modifies lir manuring, so it remains for gar- deners to do the best they can towards provid- ing other sources of potash. One of the best and most readily available is wood ash, and without knowing why, there are dozens of people who have proved it to be a valuable fertiliser. In every garden there is a general autumn burning of sticks, stems, and vegetable refuse; and it is the charred residue in the shape of the ashes that contains the potash. It is essential to preserve the latter, and it is best done by keeping it dry. If a heap of wood ashes is left out exposed through the winter to rains the best part of the potassic plant food is washed out, but if when the fire has smouldered down the dry ashes are collected and stored under cover until next spring, they are valu- able for working into the surface soil when preparing ground for sowing and planting.— "Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

div.head: THIS YEAR'S CROPS.
div.p: THIS YEAR'S CROPS.

Cereals Abundant; Hay Not §o Good. - The Board of Agriculture, reporting upon the produce of the crops in England and Wales this year, say:— The total production of wheat in England and Wales in 1914-7,318,083 quarters—is some 676,000 quarters more than last year; and the yield per acre is practically 1 bushel above the average of the past 10 years. Barley, with 32.83 bushels per acre, is a very small fraction below the aver- age, but is better than iu 1913; owing to a some- what reduced acreage, fitwever, the total pro- duction amounts to 148,300 quarters less. Oats , are half a bushel below the average, but the total production is slightly above last year's yield. Beans are practically 1 bushel over aver- , age, and the total production exceeds a million ' quarters. Peas, on the other hand, are decid- edly the worst crop, being 31 bushels below aver- age; the acreage reserved for harvesting being small, the total production (372,387 quarters) is the lowest on record.

Hay, whether from permanent grass, or from clovers and rotation grasses, is below average, the former by rather over, and the latter by rather under, 2cwt. per acre. The total produc- tion of both kinds of hay together amounts to more than 7,200,000 tons, as compared with over 9,000,000 tons in 1913, which was a very .abund- lit year. _ _
The estimate of the hay crop was issued on the sth ult., the returns of the production of pota- toes and roots are collected at a later date, and will be issued subsequently.

div.head: 1" IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: 1" IN THE GARDEN.
PROPAGATING CHRYSANTHEMUMS.

One of the most important points connected with the cUltivation of exhibition Chrysanthe- mums is the selection of the proper kind of cuttings. I prefer those which come up clear of the stem, without bud formation, and taken when about three inches long. Of course, we are obliged to resort to stem cuttings of scarce varieties. We always try to get them as near the base as possible, because the higher up the stem we get the more liable we are to have the plants showing premature buds.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

AMERICAN BLIGHT ON APPLE TREES. A friend of ours, after trying many remedies, used neatsfoot oil, painting the affected parts with this, which at once smothered up the pest. This was done when the trees were dormant, the result being that no traces of the pest have been seen since this remedy was Wed. The oil being somewhat thick, it should be slightly warmed, when with an ordinary painter's brush it can be easily worked into all the crevices. GREASE BANDS.

Now is the time when grease bands made of strips of brown paper should be put on the stems of the fruit trees at about one foot from the base of the tree, smearing these with cart grease or any sticky substance to prevent the females of the wintet moth getting into the branches. Do not put the grease on the stems of the trees. Examine the bands frequently, and, should the grease have become hard and dry, smear them a second time.—" Wick."

div.head: HYACINTHS AND TULIPS IN POTS.
div.p: HYACINTHS AND TULIPS IN POTS.

One of the most important points in the cul- tivation of these in pots is often overlooked— namely, abundance of roots before the bulbs are taken into the house. How often do we find people potting up hyacinths and other bulbs, and at once standing them on the shelf of a greenhouse, or it may be in the house window, with the result that they either rot or fail to develop their flower spikes. To guard against such failure, the bulb, when potted, should at once be plunged in ashes or leaf soil, and when it is found that the tops are showing through this covering, then it may be taken for granted that the roots are working freely in the.soil in the pots. When this happens, the bulbs may be stood in the house window with every pros- pect of their perfecting their flower spikes. The same treatment holds good in the case of hya- cinths grown in glasses, which should be stood in a dark cupboard or cellar until it is seen that the roots are clustered in the water in which the bulbs are growing, when they, too, may be brought indoors.—" Farm and Home."

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
A PARTED PAIR. Husband's Arrears Under a Separation Order. '

For being in arrears to the extent of .f.. 5 under a maintenance order granted to his wife, Ernest Green, 62, Old-road, Ashton-in-Makerfield, was charged at the Warrington County Petty Ses- sions on Wednesday, before Vice-Chancellor Stewart Smith and other magistrates. It appeared, from the evidence, that a separa- tion order had been granted to the wife, Louisa Jane Green, under which the husband was ordered to pay 15s. per week. According to the prisoner, his wages had been reduced since the order was made and he was now only getting 235. per week. Mr. Laws, the Police Court Missioner, said he saw the parties after the order had been made. He asked the man if he would pay the money through him, but he was angry, and said he did not think he had had justice. At first he said that he would not pay, but later he stated that he could not afford more than 10s. per week.
Prosecutrix (to her husband) :.Are you saving up for some artificial teeth? The Husband : No.
Prisoner was committed to prison for a month, but tlie commitment was suspended for a month in order to give him a chance of pay- ing off the arrears.

div.head: FORGIVEN, BUT DID IT AGAIN. When Stolen Fruit Was Not the Sweetest.
div.p: FORGIVEN, BUT DID IT AGAIN. When Stolen Fruit Was Not the Sweetest.

At the Oakmere Petty Sessions on Monday, before Major Wilbraham and other justices, Albert Pover and Robert Briscoe, both of Frod- sham, were charged with being found, on the night of the 10th of October, in one of the out- buildings of James Hall, farmer, of Kingsley, for an unlawful purpose.

Mr. T. S. Steel, of Warrington, who appeared to prosecute, stated that Mr. Hall was one of the largest fruit growers in Cheshire, and on the night of Saturday, the 10th October, his son had occasion to go to one of the outbuild- ings, where some three to four tons of pears and apples were stored. When entering the building he heard someone say, "Be quiet; there is somebody about." He went back to the house for his father, and on returning, with a lantern, they found the defendant Pover in the shed, lying, or leaning, against a doorway lead- ing into a barn. He had a large pocket-hand- kerchief, containing seven or eight pounds of Dears, similar to some of those in the shed, and he also had a dog with him. The pears were taken from Pover, and he was told that he would be summoned, to which he replied, "You can do what you like." He was cleared off the premises, and Mr. Hall and his son returned to the house.

div.head: ADDING INSULT TO INJURY.
div.p: ADDING INSULT TO INJURY.

About a quarter of an hour later the son went to the shed again, when he found the defendant, Briscoe, behind a lurry, in another part of the shed, lying on some straw. He explained his presence by saying that he had missed his road. He was Ordered to leave the premises, and was told that he would be sum- moned. The next morning Briscoe called at the farm and saw the prosecutor, and asked to be forgiven for being on the premises. Mr. Hall agreed to forgive him. A few minutes later, however, Briscoe was seen by Mr. Hall's son in the orchard, filling his pockets with pears, and, in consequence, Mr. Hall had de- cided to prosecute him, together with Pover. Mr. Steel pointed out that both men were known to Mr. Hall, and he had suffered in con- sequence of visits paid to his farm by men residing in the same neighbourhood as the defendants, and he (Mr. Steel) was instructed to press the charge against them. Both defendants were found guilty. Briscoe was fined 10s. and costs, and Pover was com- mitted to prison for 14 days, without the option of a fine.

div.head: STOLE FROM THE LODGER. Then Ran Away and Enlisted.
div.p: STOLE FROM THE LODGER. Then Ran Away and Enlisted.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednesday, before Messrs. J. Hayward (in the chair), C. Jackson Holm and W. T. Williams, Frederick Woodward Joynson, whose last ad- dress was given as Aldershot, was charged with stealing £7 Is. in cash and 'a safety razor, of the value of 2s. 6d., the property of John Harcourt Vernon.
Prisoner pleaded guilty to stealing the money, but not guilty to the charge of stealing the safety razor. _

The Chief Constable said that the prosecutor was the manager of the local branch of the Argenta Meat Company and was lodging with the prisoner's mother in Warrington. . On Saturday night, October 17th, when Mr. Vernon went to his lodgings, he took with him the day's takings at the shop. He placed the money under his pillow when he went to bed, •which prisoner shared with him. On the Sunday prosecutor put :the money in a box, but the following morning he discovered that it had been taken. In the meantime prisoner had absconded.

Denials Followed by Admission. The prosecutor reported the matter to the police and a warrant was taken out for pri- soner's arrest, but it was not until two days previously that it was learned that he had en- listed and as at Aldershot. The police there were communicated with and prisoner was taken into custody and brought to Warrington during the night. When he was taxed at Aldershot with regard to the charge, he uttered a strong denial, and he repeated his denial when charged in Warrington. Subsequently, however, he made an admis- sion, saying that he went to Manchester, and spent the rune; with a couple of women and then proceeded to Preston to join the Army Service Corps. Prisoner had left his work without giving any reason, and even failed to tell his mother and sister that he was going away from home.
Prisoner said he was sorry, and if the Bench would give him a chance to pay the money back again he would do so.
_ -Prisoner, who had been previously convicted this year, was sent to prison for three months, with hard labour.

Smashed a Glass Panel.--John Kilmarten, 12, Tanners-lane, was charged with having been drunk in Horsemarket-street, and also with having braken a glass panel, value 205., at the Blue Bell Inn. Prisoner put his elbow through the glass.—He was fined 55. and ordered to pay the amount of damage. Drunk in Charge.—Joseph Rowan, cab driver, 13, Dolman's-lane, was charged with having been drutik whilst in charge of a cab on Sun- day.—lt was stated that 'prisoner was driving the cab up the centre of the Market-place. As there was no exit an officer stopped prisoner and found that he WA& drunk.—The Chief. Con- stable said prisoner had committed a similar offence in May, and if he carried on like lie had been doing, it was doubtful whether the police would recommend him for a licence again.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.

Mr DEAR CHILDREN,— There seems to be no end of the great war in sight. Without doubt, it will continue for some time yet, and, as it result, there will be thousands of unhappy homes during the winter. Those of you who are in a position to help others should not fail to do your best, for if you do all you can there is no doubt that many a little boy and girl will be made happy. We are drawing near to the special season of the year, when we should make every endeavour to scatter seeds of kindness and goodwill. That season is Christmastide, so do all you can to help those who are not so well off as yourselves. You can do no more.

As I hays said before, we in the British Isles have every reason to be proud of our silors and soldiers. If it were not for them the Germans would have been here long ago. We know that we can have faith in our brave men.
Your loving UNCLE NED.
HOW KHAKI WAS DISCOVERED.

Now that we see so many men about the town who are dressed in the familiar khaki uniform, it is of interest to note how the dye now used was discovered. The British troops in India wore a cotton uniform, which, when it was new, was khaki in colour, but the dye faded away when the uni- form was washed. A Manchester business man happened to remark that a fortune awaited the man who could find a khaki dye that neither sun, soap, nor soda would fade. A young officer heard the remark, hired a skilful native dyer, and began the search. Years passed without any success from their numerous experiments. However, one day, when they were turning over a heap of rags, relics of their failures, they came across one piece which was still khaki, although it had been washed several times.

The cloth had received no special treatment, sd far as they knew, except that it had fallen into a metal dish. That was the secret. The metal of the dish and the chemicals in the dye had combined to produce the fadeless khaki colour which makes our soldiers almost in- visible at a distance, and turned the young officer into a millionaire.

div.head: DISTINGUISHED DOG.
div.p: A DISTINGUISHED DOG.

There have been many famous dogs, but prob- ably none have gained greater distinction than one named Prohaska, which belonged to an Austrian regiment bearing that name. The dog was present at the storming of Vicen in 1848, and was mentioned in official dispatchas as being among the wounded. Prohaska took his Place at the head of the corps at the com- mencement of the battle, and as the firing was going on he ran from one end to the other bark- ing all the time. His behaviour brightened the spirits of the soldiers, and when the regiment charged their enemy he still kept in front. It was then that he received his injuries. In four different battles he was wounded, but each time he had been attended to he ran to the front of the regiment again. The officers and men were so delighted with the dog that an application was made to head- quarters to make the dog a corporal. Permis- sian was granted, and the stripes were fixed to his collar. In 1849 Prohaska accompanied the advance

REV. A. M. MITCHELL AND MR. DENNETT'S " FUNNY" SPEECH.
The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning, Mr. A. J. Jolley pre- siding.

div.head: MAKING THEM USEFUL.
div.p: MAKING THEM USEFUL.
It was reported that the boys in the Padgate Homes had been taught how to darn, and that they now darned their own stockings.
THE COST OF THE POOR LAW CHILD.

The Superintendent of the Children's Homes reported that the average cost of maintenance per head per week for the year was ss. 10d., as against 6s. 1.6 d. for the previous year. Miss Broadbent said the report was satisfac- tory. _

Mr. Brooks: When the superintendent sub- mitted his first report it was stated that the reduced expenditure was brought about by the large stocks he had in at that time. That ex- cuse cannot be made this time, because the large stocks were not there all the while. It is very gratifying to note that the superintendent has kept the expenses down. We ought to give honour where honour is due.

Mr. Dale: We ought to be very glad that we have such a superintendent and matron to look after that institution, and we all realise that in this case economy and efficiency go arm in arm. The Chairman added his tribute to the valu- able work which had been done. Mr. and Mrs. Lawrence had, he said, shown themselves worthy of the confidence of the Board. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Long may they reign! CHILDREN'S HOMES TO BE IMPROVED.

With reference to the Guardians' proposal to make structural alterations at the Padgate Homes, the Local Government Board wrote stat- ing that • any proposal for the erection of an- other building at Padgate for children between the ages of three and five would be favourably considered.
Mr. Mather said that was satisfactory, and showed that the Chairman's prophecy was com- ing true.
it was decided that the necessary arrange- ments for the building be left in the hands of the Padgate Homes Committee. Several altera- tions and improvements will be made. "WEARY WILLIES'" BREAD.

In regard to the new order as to the provision of bread stations, a communication was read to the effect that, whilst proper arrangements were being made, the vagrants' wards should be used in the meantime.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell : We are going to incur additional expense without any additional advantage. These men will get their bread before they leave the institution, and will eat it as soon as they get outside. They will still call on private houses, and do as they have done in the past. The arrangement is an un- satisfactory one, and the sooner it is terminated the better.

The Chairman: If the police authorities and Guardians work together it will be successful. The arrangement suggested is only temporary. If the police, magistrates, Guardians, and the public would co-operate, vagrancy could be stamped out altogether. It is a great nuisance, and it can be stopped. The system is working well in some parts, and ought to go well here. Mrs. Collingwood : When proper notices are issued to say where vagrants can get food, the public will co-operate gladly. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: They will steal our hearts then.
The Chairman: It is a good thing to have a soft heart but not a soft head. (Laughter.)

THE PROPOSED NEW OFFICES. It was reported that at a meeting of the Building Committee the Clerk read a letter, dated October 21st, from the Town Clerk of Warrington, informing the Guardians that the Council had acquired a plot of land adjoining the site of the new Board room offices in Museum-street, and, as arranged, a draft agree- ment would be prepared under which the Cor- poration would give the Guardians a right a way over a passage to be constructed between the offices and any building which blight be erected on the land acquired by the Corpora- thin, on the understanding that the Guardians would set back their proposed offices from Win- marleigh-street. The minutes were confirmed. WHY HE WAS ABSENT! _

Mr. Dennett referred to the discussion at the last meeting of the Board with reference to the absence of members, and explained that on three consecutive meeting days he colt not attend on account of sickness. Afterwa s the harvest was on, labour was scarce, and—well, one must make hay whilst the sun shone! He had to look after his business. He had not missed once through spending holidays in coun- tries which were now having to fight. He lived some distance away from the Workhouse, and , he had not a carriage and pair. 'I am here to be reprimanded," concluded Mr. Bennett. "1 think of the members who have attended most, Mr. Mitchell is the best. I know one clergyman, the Rector of Lymm, who has been on the Coun- cil for a number of years. He has resigned, his duties being so heavy. If their duties are so heavy, I think they can ill-afford to attend meet- ings very regularly." The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: That is rather too funny! Might I say that before Mr. Dennett put up as a candidate, he ought to have taken into account and carefully considered whether or not—harvest and sowing time being taken into account—he was really justified in undertaking Guardians' work. • I think he has given him- self away this morning, and I think he would resign if he did the right thing, and allow an- other man to take his place. lam quite as hard a worker as Mr. Bennett, but if I lie in bed, as so mink people do, and sleep for seven or eight hours, I could not get through with my work and attend the Board of Guardians as well. I take less sleep, and therefore I am able to get through my duties without neglect. Mr. Bennett: Is it customary amongst clergy to do with seven or eight hours' sleep?, Mr. Flanagan: I was in a town last week, and this had been discussed, and one man said, "If you don't attend you don't do as much harm as those who do." (Laughter.) Miss Broadbent: Why should Mr. Bennett be made the scapegoat, whilst there are other old offenders on the Board who could be mentioned.

"YOU HAVE GOT SACKED NOW."

What we have preached from Labour and Socialist platforms for years as to the identity of the Liberals and-Tories has been made plain to you during this election. They have proved their identity of interests. It is a case of Tweedledee and Tweedledum every time. When your boss or employer gives you the boot, and you want men to fight your battles at the works gates—(a Voice: "Go home")—where are these men? (There were several interjections at this point.) I never got sacked from a job in my life. (A Voice: "You have got sacked now," and laughter.) Let this be underAtood by the public. All I want—(Voices: "Three cheers for Mr. Dickenson.") The crowd then spontaneously commenced to sing the National Anthem, and Mr. Dukes and the other defeated candidates were requested to leave the Town Hall steps. Councillor Halliwell next spoke a few words to the crowd. He said: I thank you once again for your votes. I may say that this is the third time that I have fought Orford, and I have fought three Socialists, and every time my majorities have increased. If they come again I will beat them by still more. I again thank you. (Cheers.)

div.head: CHEERS AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: CHEERS AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

When the tidings of the sweeping victories secured by their two candidates at the polls was conveyed to the large company of mem- bers gathered in the Liberal Club there were hearty outbursts of cheering, but there was nothing in the shape of speechmaking. The truce was observed even to this extent.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL CONSERVATIVE
div.p: THE SUCCESSFUL CONSERVATIVE
Rousing Club Reception for Councillor , _

At the Conservative Club, Councillor Lash- ford was warmly congratulated on his victory, and in the course of a speech in the billiard

Mr. T. Fulton-Smith said: We must congratu- late Councillor Lashford on his success to-day— on his success in helping to smash the Social- ists. The best thing to do with them is to send them to Germany to get their Christmas goose; if they can find food there at the time. (Laugh- ter.) Councillor Lashford has rendered a good service in trying to break up this society, who would try to smash up the whole community. They are no credit to themselves, and it is a great shame that they should be allowed to stop in the country and upset towns as they have been allowed to do far too long. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: 'SOCIALISTS NOT WANTED.
div.p: 'SOCIALISTS NOT WANTED.

Councillor Lashford said:, I have been suc- cessful in three contests in St. John's Ward, a thing which no other individual ,has accom- plished. I have topped the majority of the late Mr. John Magian. His majority was 641 and my majority is 647. I have put my faith in the electors of St. John's Ward, and they have shown that they won't have the Socialist party to represent them in the Warrington Town Council. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

'I stand here, one of the proudest men who ever put up in St. John's Ward," was Coun- cillor Lashford's opening sentence at the Junior Conservative Club, where there was a large attendance. He thanked the Conservatives,and Liberals for the work they had done for him. (Hear, hear.) He could not say he thanked the Conservatives alone, because a large number of the Liberals had done their best. During the next three years he would do his utmost to better what he had done in the past six years. (Hear, bear.) People in St. John's did not want a Socialist representative. (Voices: "We don't want them," and "We won't have them.") He thought it was idiotic for the Socialists to have contested three wards in the present crisis. The three men who had been returned were three of the working men's can- didates. He had always stood for the working men. (A Voice: "You cannot say the Social- ists are for the working men !")

SOCIALISTS ALIAS LABOURITE. Councillor McKee said that Councillor Lashford had stood for everything that was for the betterment of the working classes, and a large majority of the people in that ward were of the working classes, who had to work hard for their living. Councillor Lashford's large majority would give him an impetus to carry on his work with greater zeal. The fight had been an unnecessary one. The Social- ist party, masquerading under the name of the Labour party, had got what they deserved for working the elections at this time of crisis. This country was fighting the biggest Social- istic country in the world; an enemy which had been preparing for the last ton or fifteen years. The people were not thinking now so much about home or municipal matters—pav- ing, street lighting, &c.—as about the soldiers at the front. (Hear, hear.) As loyal people they did not want to see those contests at the municipal hustings, but a fight had been forced upon them by the Socialist party, who really wanted seats without fighting. The public of Warrington did not want the Socialists to have those seats. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Dukes had said there were 143 who did. (A Voice: "Christian people.") He had said, at any rate, that his party would contest any election in the future. Well, it would be a case of God help them if they went to St. John's Ward. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: "NO POLITICS!"
div.p: "NO POLITICS!"

Mr. Joseph Taylor said he was pleased at the manner in which sorae of their opponents had worked. They had rendered assistance which had been very helpful, especially in No. 6 Sec- tion. The ladies had also rendered yeoman service. He hoped he would have the same band of workers for Mr. Harold Smith at the next election. (A Voice: "No party politics !") The Liberal party had been as true as steel and had kept to their compact that there should be no fight. He asked—Was the present a time when they should waste money? He could take Mr. Charles Dukes to homes in Town's End where the moneythat had beenwasted on this elec- tion could be more usefully spent. (Hear, hear.) He took second place to no Charlie Dukes, nor any member of his party. He met one of that element a fortnight ago and he talked about what was being done whilst the soldiers were away. One of "the vermin" threw it at him that it paid Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall to do what they were doing, because they saw that if the Germans came here they would lose all their wealth, and Walton Hall would be razed to the ground as homes in Belgium had been. (A Voice: "Don't make party politics of it !") He was speaking of the Socialists and not of politics, which had been sunk by both parties. His idea of real Sialism was doing all one could for the betterrlent and uplifting of those who were unable to help themselves. In conclusion, the speaker said the electors

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1914.
had done a great deal of good in dismissing the three Socialists and so stopping the rotten game of spending money that was not needed.
In 2,'9 boxes only, six boxes 1319, 411 chem

div.head: AFTER DEFEAT. Labour Candidates ludulge In Evian-
div.p: AFTER DEFEAT. Labour Candidates ludulge In Evian-
ation .and Invedive.
At the Socialist Hall the three defeated can- didates were given -a hearty welcome by • a large crowd.
BEATEN-BUT PLEASED!

Mr. J. Helsby said that he was pleased for the first time in his life to stand before them as a defeated candidate. It was not everybody who had pleasure in being defeated, but he might say that if the three men who had been returned to the Council were a sample of the Town Coun- cil in general, he, for one, was glad that he had not got in. That was because it had always been his maxim to try to get into better company. He was convinced that the company of the Town Council, judging from those who had got in that day, was not fit company for him. The Trades Council candidates had put up a good fight under very adverse circumstances. The elec- tion had not been fought on municipal matters, but upon the international crisis. They had had to face the whole weight of the Liberal and Tory parties; they had had to fight the money bags of Warrington, and they had not had the support they should have received from the trade union movement. (Hear, hear.) He was very sorry that he had to admit it. In his own cake he had had members of his own trade union working strenuously against him. He seriously thought that had the union which had nomin- ated him stuck to him, they would have carried St. John's Ward flying, because the Insnrance Agents had a great weight, no matter where they threw it. As he had said before, there were 143 righteous souls in St. John's Ward, 143 who dared call their souls their own. (Hear, hear.) They could always count upon the backing of 143 votes in that ward on any occasion, because they could not have fought under more adverse circumstanCes. (Hear, hear.) They (the Labour men) had run their elections on £l7 or .218, and yet they had put up a good fight. " A Dirty Filthy False Poster!"

They were tied down by the Trades and Labour Council in the first instance not to exceed .RlO. They were under the impression from statements which had appeared in the Press and elsewhere that their opponents did not desire to enter into controversy. They took their word for granted, thinking they would only have to pay for polling cards and an elec- tion address. However, their opponents issued a dirty, filthy, false poster—his adjectives were not strong enough—and the Labour candidates had had to reply. They had, he thought, really come out with flying colours, because there was not another town in England where men would have _gone through such a fight, never mind not getting in. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had been put to a greater expense than they at first anticipated, and he therefore asked every trade unionist present to see that his society paid their.little share towards the £lB. 37 VOTES—BUT NOT DOWNHEARTED! Mr. A. E. Seabury said that as the candidate who was nominated by the British Socialist party he was very pleased that he had fought. (Bear, hear, and applause.) They had put up a good fight, and he was not downhearted. His heart was in the same place now as it was before the election. It had not put him out, but he would not like to " swop" his heart for Dicken- son's heart. (Laughter.) He (the speaker) en- dorsed all that Comrade Helsby had said. It gave him the greatest satisfaction to realise that there were 37 people in Bewsey Ward who were not afraid of the name Socialist. (Applause.) MR. DUKES SAYS TRAPS WERE SET FOR

div.head: HIM.
div.p: HIM.

Mr. C. Dukes said that he had already had one innings outside the Town Hall, and had been denied the freedom of speech. Whilst walking down to those rooms he had heard remarks from his colleagues as to what might and might not have been said. He had carried something under his waistcoat, so to speak, in this fight, and he did not mind telling the gathering then that if .Rl,OOO could have incriminated Dukes in a libel action, it would have been spent. Traps had been set for him and those things had occu- pied his mind. Such a fight was calculated to tax the energies of the most strenuous man. He knew that those things had been, and were yet, at work, and it was simply because of that that his language had been deliberately chosen, in order to give the men concerned no 'handle. He left his hearers to draw their own conclusions. He was before that meeting as a man who had been educated and produced by the class to which those in the room that night belonged. He went into the movement as a young man, and had allied himself with the spirit of what it meant. He was giving good advice to the young men present when he said that he, too, had had the same aspirations as they had when he first interested himself, not as a candidate, in municipal affairs. He would pass on the ad- vice of a crusted old Tory, who once said to him, "Young fellow, you don't know the forces you are up against." When

They were simply asking for the Socialist movement and realising that they must expect a concentration of forces against them—a desire to spend money against them—and they must also expect to see their enemies ever prepared to single out the men who had dared to chal- lenge their right to represent the people, as they called it. When a Socialist got in the Council he would not be there to nod his head when the string was pulled. He would be there as a critic and would he viewed as such by their opponents. They had polled a very small minority, but to the men who had voted in their favour every credit was due. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They must not forget that where they got a man prepared to take a certain line of action industrially, that man would take a similar line, for or against, in the Political world. But when they had got to get a worker to transfer his thoughts to municipal affairs they were asking him to think, and, hard as it was to say it, lie had to confess that they had got very few thinking people. "A House Divided Against Itself." -

"The people to-day," Mr. Dukes continued, "ape what the gods that be lay down. Men see a placard on the wall and 99 per cent, of them will take that as though it were gospel ! We have men in our own movement who do not believe we were justified in fighting; therefore, how much was to be expected from other people?" They had, he went-on, fought Warrington, not in a municipal contest, but on the international crisis, and they had been tackling the things which the statesmen of the Continent were dealing with. The only virtue in the fight had been this—that they had dared to fight when it was unpopular, at a time when their own colleagues of the Independent Labour party said they ought not to fight, because they would lose prestige. "And," added Mr. Dukes, "it is only a few years ago that men were .stoned because they belonged to the Independent Labour party !" „

He did not believe there were two other married men in Warrington who dared have undertaken the responsibility with him in the fight, and if there was only one man who had been converted and said that from henceforth he would be a Socialist, they would be amply rewarded for the trouble they had undertaken. kApplause.)
BOUQUET FOR COUNCILLOR-DICKENSON. At the close of the poll in the Bewsey Ward, Councillor Dickenson was presented with a handsome bouquet of chrysanthemums by a number of lady supporters.

div.head: LOSS OF TEN YEARS' WORK.
div.p: LOSS OF TEN YEARS' WORK.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

_ Sir,—The Labour Council has fought and the picture has told its own story, and I would that the Labour members of the town should charge its government with a wilful disregard of the obligations entrusted to them. Mr. Dukes, their honest servant, I could freely forgive—" for all good secretaries do as they are told "—if it was not for the fact that he is the master mind of the party in economics, and must have known the seriousness of such a blunder. It was his privilege to advise, or he may have respectfully declined to stand, with honour to himself and in the interest of those who employ him. As a trade unionist I feel ashamed at the result. In my opinion, they have undone ten years' clean, honest, hard work in the cause. Hoping that the lesson will have the effect of making them more 'careful in the future.— Yours, &c., "THE ROAD MENDER."

div.head: MISSIONARY PROBLEMS.
div.p: MISSIONARY PROBLEMS.
Canada and China the "Biggest Propositions."
BIG LOCAL MEETING.

"People speak of the present war as Armaged- don, but I am inclined to think that, perhaps, the final Armageddon will be the great clash of the yellow and white races of the world." In these words, Dr. Graham Aspland, the medical missionary, who has seen service in several parts of the globe, urged upon a large audience, assembled in the Co-operative Hall, on Tuesday evening, the need for continuing and increasing Christian missionary effort in the vast Chinese territory. The meeting was called in support of the claims of the Foreign Missions of the Church of England, and was presided over by the Rev. and Hon. C. F. Cross, who was supported by the Rev. Archdeacon 'Evans and Dr. Graham Aspland (as a deputation from headquarters), the Revs. Canon Willis, J. H. G. Hollingworth, James Collins, and others.

div.head: WRONG WAY OF SOLVING THE LABOUR PROBLEM.
div.p: WRONG WAY OF SOLVING THE LABOUR PROBLEM.
After a few brief introductory remarks by the Chairman,

Archdeacon Evans dealt in a most interesting manner with the work of the Universities Mis- sion to Central Africa—a branch of missionary effort with which he has been long and honour- ably associated. He began by telling how the Universities Mission was a response to Living- stone's cry on behalf of the slaves, and went on to explain that the notoirious slave trade of Cen- tral Africa was an attempt to solve a labour pro- blem. There was always a labour problem in Africa. Wherever there was a commodity like, say, rubber to be gathered, or gold to be dug, and the climate and general conditions were such that the people who held the country for profit could not gather or dig the commodity for themselves, there was always a tendency to the introduction of a system of slavery. The Uni- versities Mission were the pioneers in the work of abolishing slavery in East Africa; it was their • influence which got that terrible ban brought to an end in Zanzibar, East Africa and Central Africa, and to-day, although there were no slaves, the work was done just the same, and, what was more, it had been proved that free labour was much cheaper than slave labour, for it had to be remembered that it was one thing to get a slave and another matter altogether to make him work. Sometimes, the speaker con- tinued, the Universities Mission were asked what they were doing in German East Africa.

div.head: German Generosity.
div.p: German Generosity.

His reply to that was: What are the Germans doing in the portion of Africa which is worked by the Universities Missions, for the Missions were in that part of Africa twenty years before the Germans came. Still, he wanted to be fair to the Germans, and to say that they had never made their coming a hindrance to the work of the 'Missions; on the contrary, they had for- warded to the U.M. Office in London all the money which they collected as custom dues on Mission goods going into their territory. Describing the daily work of the missionary, the speaker said one had not to be living among the African heathen, nor, indeed, among any other peoples, before he realised that conscience was an endowment of all human nature, and it was with the conscience that the work of the missionary began. On the religious side the mis- sionary found that he had little to upset in the way of settled beliefs, but on the social side—as, for instance, when it came to dealing with the question of polygamy—he found himself up against a stiffer proposition, and the aim of the missionary was to take hold of the unconverted at the point of development which they had reached and lead them on from that to higher things.
Novel .Offertory Contributions.

Their great hope for the future, the speaker went on, was a self-governing, self-supporting church in Africa. It would amuse an English congregation to see the churchwardens go round for the collections at some of the Universities Missions' churches. They did not take plates; they took sacks, into which the faithful dropped fowls and potatoes and such like comestibles. (Laughter.) The churchwardens used those things much in the same way as the wardens at home used the money given them under the heading, "church expenses." The war, continued the speaker, had taught one thing. They had seen in the papers how that 1,200 English clergymen had volunteered to go to the front as chaplains. Did not that show that the Church at home could apparently easily spare 1,200 men; that there need not in normal times be any shortage of missionaries in the for- , eign field, that home ties could be left, if need be. If twelve hundred men could be spared to play their part in the earthly warfare; surely half that number might have been spared for the higher warfare.

div.head: ENGLAND "ALWAYS PLAYS UP."
div.p: ENGLAND "ALWAYS PLAYS UP."

Dr. Graham Aspland, who was introduced by the Chairman as " no stranger to Warrington," began by saying that England was a good old country—" she always plays up to you when you are in difficulties." And so it was, in spite of the war, for subscriptions to the S.P.G. were more than £lO,OOO up at the end. of last month, and that notwithstanding the fact that last year there was an increase in subscriptions and donations of over £34,000, as compared with the previous year. (Applause.) He appealed to his hearers not to let missionary enterprises suffer because of the war, adding " You are not going to, because you are British; you dare not do so, because you are Christians." There was one person who was worse than a Little Englander, and that was a Little Churchman. (Hear, hear.) The speaker went on to review the work of the Society, and of missions in general in different parts of the globe. Canada, he said, presented, perhaps, the greatest problem the S.P.G. had to face, and as it was a problem for which, in the main, Britain was responsible, the British people, whatever they might do for China, Africa and India, had got to do something for their great North-Western Colony.

div.head: Africa—The Great Challenge.
div.p: Africa—The Great Challenge.

If Canada was the greatest problem; if Canada was a great opportunity for the Church at home, then Africa was the great challenge. Canada gave them an opportunity of showing what their faith could do and ought to do; Africa presented them with a challenge to do it. The speaker proceeded to give some interesting statistics. Out of every twenty missionaries in the world, he said, thirteen were Roman Catho- lics and six were Nonconformists. Had the Catholics a greater or better faith? Had the creedless churches a greater hold upon God; was their devotion to Christ greater than that of the Churchpeople? Yet the Churchpeople had only one missionary out of every twenty, and in order to make-up that proportion the whole of Greater Britain had to be taken into the reckoning. Turning to Africa, the speaker said that in huge tracts of that vast Continent they found Mohammedanism challenging Christianity—the Crescent pitted against the Cross; and it looked as if the Crescent was going to win, because the Mohammedan religion produced something greater and stronger of devotion and sacrifice among its adherents than did Christianity.

div.head: India After The War.
div.p: India After The War.

Great as it was already, continued the speaker, the problem of India would be a still greater one after the war was over. Were they going to use the native troops to fight for England, and then deny the race to which they belonged the liberty they had been wanting for the last twenty years; were they going to give them a voice in their own national affairs?

_ Speaking of China, Dr. Aspland said that it might seem an astounding statement to make, but, nevertheless, it was quite true, that Chris- tianity was the most popular religion in China I just now. The Chinese, he continued, were going to be a great military people; they were going to develop in every department of national life. They must find a place in the comity of the world somewhere, and the pro- blem for the Churches was: Shall they • find that place as Christians, or as materialists? People talked of the present war as Armaged- don, but he was inclined to think that, perhaps, the final Armageddon of time would be the great clash of the yellow and white races of the world. The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman and speakers, proposed by the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth and seconded by the Rev. James Collins.
The sum of £l2 us. 6d. was collected at the meeting.

div.head: CHURCHES AND THE WAR.
div.p: CHURCHES AND THE WAR.
THE WAR AND CHURCH OFFER- TORIES.

Writing in the current issue of the St. Ann's Parish Magazine, the Vicar (the Rev. James Davies) issues the following "Note of Warn- ing " : " Do not let 'the war' excuse your giving. God's work needs not only our usual but in- creased support that it may be more efficient and more widespread •than ever, so that the Kingdom of our Lord may be strengthened and extended. We repeat that we should and must as a duty and a privilege make sacrifices on account of the war, to suppose those called to arms and risking limbs and life and shedding blood and giving lives for us, but let it be 'self- sacrifice,' that which costs us something, not a transferring of our gifts to God's work to the War Funds."

div.head: LAST GREAT BATTLE. When .ancl, Where Will Armaueddon Be Fought?
div.p: THE LAST GREAT BATTLE. When .ancl, Where Will Armaueddon Be Fought?

"The present war, a fulfilment of prophecy and its issue certain. What it means as to the future, and how it affords a complete vindica- tion of Christadelphian teaching." Such was the outline of a lecture entitled "Is it Arma- geddon?" delivered to a large audience by Mr. G. H. Denny, of Walsall, on Monday evening, at the Christadelphian Meeting Room, Bold- street. I Mr. Joseph P. Jennings, who presided, having explained the object of the lecture, read as an introduction Daniel vii.—the chapter describ- ing the vision of the four beasts and its inter- pretation. He then called upon Mr. Denny to proceed. The lecturer said that whilst all, he took it, were agreed as to the desirability for the coming of peace and goodwill amongst men, and the complete ingathering to the Church, the Cliris tadelphians argued from the Scriptures that the Kingdom of God could only comp by the re-visitation of Jesus Christ. Instead of im- proving, the world was going back; and now practically tht whole of it was full of strife. German "Culture" the Essence of Barbarism. Where was civilisation? Culture, as the Ger- mans understood it, had proved to be the very essence of barbarism. Having departed from the beliefs of Christianity, Nebuchadnezzar lost his power for seven years. At length he con- fessed that earthly power was given by God alone, and he was restored to his position (Daniel iv. 34). The repulsive, bestial nature of the Babylonian Empire was then changed to a new and better understanding. He (the speaker) maintained that the kingdoms of this earth had been established by the same bestial methods. The speaker endeavoured to show by means of diagrams that Nebuchadnezzar's vision of the image represented the Babylonian, Medo- Persian, Grecian and Imperial Roman Empires. The last—" iron" as Gibbon called it—was the greatest the world had ever known. Yet all these had passed away. The prophecies said that the Kingdom of God was to supplant all these. They also clearly showed that the ten toes of the image represented Portugal, Spain, France, -Belgium, Holland, Germany, Austria, Russia, Italy and Switzerland—no more and no less. Germany was endeavouring to weld all these into one, but it was prophesied that they should all remain separate until the second advent of Christ.

England and Russia the Last Protagonists. In Ezekiel =Evil. they saw how the dead hope of Israel was revived by the resurrection of dry bones, after which came the promises of Christ's kingdom. Thus they found that the Jews now were flocking back in great numbers to Pales- tine—which was the central land of all the world. Their hope came from the recent words of the Chief Rabbi: " The fact that the British people have stood in to keep their treaty obliga- tions is a proof that they will do the same for the Jews." This, said the speaker, was also prophesied. The first piece of work of any character that Lord Kitchener did was to inspect Palestine, which he described as an ideal battlefiehl: here. as prophecy made quite clear, would be fought the last great battle in this world—Armaged- don! As had been said, Russia would pull Ger- many's ramshackle empire piece from piece. She would become the predominating Power in Europe, and Britain would oppose her concern- ing Palestine. They would then he on the threshold of the final things, for the time limit of Biblical prophecy was 1942. Thus they should thank God that there was a way out of the darkness and storm; that they might know it was truly His will working out; and that, when earthly rule had failed, they were approaching the times of heavenly rule.
The Chairman thanked the audience for their presence and attention.

div.head: WHAT ENGLAND FORGETS!
div.p: WHAT ENGLAND FORGETS!
Rev. Bryan iifown anti the \Nicety(' Church.

The Rev. W. Bryan Brown, who, eleven years ago, held a mission at St. Peter's, Warrington, paid that church another visit on Wednesday, when be preached at the weekly evening ser- vice, taking fer his text: "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen" . .

(Dent. iv. 9). - Having reminded his hearers of Rudyard Kip- ling's words after the Boer War: "Lord God of Hosts, be with us yet; lest we forget!" the preacher said that some of them would like to forget many things, but they should be careful what they allowed to be stamped upon their memories—that which they heard and read and saw. What was meant by memory? • That which-was stamped upon the brain, and thus upon the heart! It was a good thing to learn hymns and psalms, and to recite these over to themselves now and then. The noble words would make them forget evil things.

The War, A Lesson From God. And to their land this day they might say: "Take heed !" God was teaching it lessons by this war, which could be taught in no other way; and those lessons must not be forgotten. What had England forgotten in the past? She had been forgetting the House of God! The Warrington Parish Church taught a fine lesson —its tall steeple pointing up to heaven. And they should not be content as buttresses out- side the church they should be pillars inside it. When they heard the church bells ringing, they should look up and say, "I was glad when they said unto me: Let us go into the House
Continued in next column.

div.head: Street, Oxford Street, London, W. Refuse substitutes.
div.p: Street, Oxford Street, London, W. Refuse substitutes.
buying now, they would keep St. Peter's flag flying. He wished the, church all success. (Applause.) Mr. T. REDD/SEI seconded, and the motion was carried with acclamation.
In acknowledgment, Miss Warn said she hoped they would all follow Mr. Steel's motto. _ _
Tuesday's takings amounted to £6l 75., and the total sum raised was £l3l Is. sd.—a credit- able result.

div.head: "BUSINESS AS USUAL."
div.p: "BUSINESS AS USUAL."
St. Peter's Church Adopts the
Trade Motto.
SUCCESSFUL SALE OF WORK.

The members of the St. Peter's Church, War- rington, have been having a busy time this week, for on Monday and Tuesday they held their annual sale of work in the John-street Schoolroom, on behalf of the parish parochial organisations. . .

The Rev. B. Percival (vicar) occupied the chair on Monday, when the sale was declared open by Miss Buckton. There were also pre- sent: The Revs. John Martin (curate) and H. V. l'igot; Mesdames Carleton, Percival, Pigot and Willis; and Messrs. G. E. Greaves (sides- man), E. A. Padmore (organist and choirmaster) and T. Readish (people's warden).

div.head: BIG ANNUAL SUM REQUIRED.
div.p: BIG ANNUAL SUM REQUIRED.

The CHAIRMAN said that some of his parish- ioners had suggested the abandonment of this year's sale owing to the war. The nation's motto, however, was "Business as usual," and they would follow it. They had to raise a large sum every year for their various organ- isations; the Curates' and Layworkers' Funds required £245 each year, and they were not endowed. As a result of these voluntary efforts, they gave last year £63 to the Curates' Fund; £25 to the Church Army Captains' Fund; £l5 to the Churchwardens' Fund; and £l2 to other organisations; besides ..e6 10s. to building repairs. In introducing Miss Buck- ton, the Chairman said that she belonged to a well-known family, whose interest in St. Peter's was great, and who kindly gave £3OO, some years ago, to increase the endowment of the church. That resulted in it getting £3OO more from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. It was also interesting to note that Miss Buckton's brother, the Rev. Harold Buckton, was their first curate after the rebuilding of the church. (Applause.)

THE PLEASURE THAT IS THE WORKERS'. Miss BUCKTON thanked Mr. Percival for the very kind manner in which he had spoken of her family and its work. She had been deeply interested in hearing about the distrilmtion of the church funds. Workers had to experience many difficulties and anxieties, but these they did not mind, because there were many plea- , sures also, which only workers could under- stand. At the same time, she was sorry that they had additional anxiety as to how expenses were to be met, and she trusted their efforts would be highly successful. (Applause.) Mr. T. Rentasit moved, and Mr. GEORGE E. GREAVES seconded, a sincere vote of thanks to Miss Buckton, the Vicar also being compli- mented on his excellent organisation of parish affairs.

div.head: motion was then carried. The proceeds on Monday totalled £69 14s. sd. THE SECOND DAY.
div.p: The motion was then carried. The proceeds on Monday totalled £69 14s. sd. THE SECOND DAY.

Again there was a large gathering on Tuesday afternoon, when Miss White opened the sale, the Vicar presiding. There were also present on the platform the Revs. Canon Morley Stev- enson and, John Martin; Mesdames Carleton, James Fairclough, John Fairclough, Henry Greenall, Percival and Pigot ; the Misses Buck- ton and Smethurst; and Messrs. T. S. Steel and T. Reddish (churchwardens). Having announced the result of Monday's sale,

The CHAIRMAN said be would like to mention that, this year, they missed one who had always taken a great interest in their • work. He re- ferred to Mr. 13amforth, their lay representa- tive, whose help they at St. Peter's had found unfailing, especially at their sales of work. He would like to thank the workers; when they remembered that many of them had been with them right through all these functions, they could specially appreciate their assistance. He went on to introduce Miss White, who had come to open the sale, remarking that he ought to mention that the late Dr. White had always attended their sales, and took a great interest in their work. They all gave Miss White a very hearty welcome. (Applause.)

div.head: KEEP PAROCHIAL WORK GOING.
div.p: KEEP PAROCHIAL WORK GOING.

SEES WHITE thanked the Chairman for his kind words and those present for their cordial reception. She knew that at this time there were many calls upon them, but she thought that the work they did for the soldiers and sailors should not be allowed to make their ordinary work suffer. She was very glad to hear that so far the sale had been such a suc- cess, and trusted it would be as successful on that, the second, day as it was on the first. (Applause.) . .

T. S. STEEL proposed a Very hearty vote of thanks to Miss White, who, he said, had always taken a great interest in their work. They all hoped this sale would not fall below the level of those gone by. As he came along to attend the opening ceremony, he saw the following notice in a shop window :
"Keep on buying; Keep the flag flying!" That. applied to their sale. By keeping on
CHURCHES AND THE WAR—continued.

of the Lord." The House of God was the gate of heaven; and how could they expect to enter His heavenly home if they neglected His earthly one? There were many, too, who went to church, but who turned their backs upon the most precious part of the service—the Holy Communion. Jesus had said: "Do this in re- membrance of me"; it was His last wish, and they should therefore obey it.

The Desecration of the Sabbath. Again, God had set apart a day specially for Himself, and, if they did not devote it to Him, they were robbing God! Many townspeople passed their Sundays by walking in the country. Well, there could be no objection to that, if they would only attend the early morning and the evening services. "A Sunday well spent Brings a week of content," it had been said; and that ivas true, for it car- ried its influence into their home life. They were soldiera, of God, engaged in war- fare against the world, the flesh and the devil; and how could they hope to conquer the enemy if they did not have plenty Of sword practice? The Bible was their sword. If they, as a nation, would only listen to the voice of God, and humble themselves before him, the war would speedily be concluded.

div.head: £lOO FOR THE PARISH CHURCH. Satisfactory Result of One Day Sale.
div.p: £lOO FOR THE PARISH CHURCH. Satisfactory Result of One Day Sale.

The Warrington Parish Church sale of work was held on Thursday in the Fairfield School. "It is hoped," the Rector had written in his Parish Magazine, "that all parishioners will do their best to make the day a great success, so that whilst working for our soldiers and sailors, our church may not have to suffer from want of funds." Although no special effort was made —the object being only to sell those articles made before the start of the war—the efforts of the congregation were very successful, for .e 75 was raised, and a kind subscription of .R 25 from Lady Greenall raised the total to ..tlOO. The sale was well attended, the Rector open- ing it with prayer. Later, afternoon tea and supper were provided. The following were the stall-holders:— Rectory Stall.—Mesdames Willis and Peter Rylands, Miss Shaw. , Congregational Stall.—Mesdames Craik, Bot- tomley, Farrall. Scott, and others. Institute Stall.—Mesdames Webster, Price, Tilling, Bolton, Brandreth, Owen, Jones, Miss Baldwin. Flower Stall.—Miss Profit. Girls' F.S. Stall.—Mesdames Locker and Lunt, Misses Winstanley and Dannett. Tea Room.—Misses Cooper, Lawrence, Isher- wood, Whittle and others. St. Clement's Stall.—Mesdames Hickson and hail. St. George's Stall.—Mesdames Knight and Harburn.

div.p: IN A GOOD CAUSE. Sale of Work to Raise Funds for St. Hilda's Mission.

In aid of the St. llilda's Mission Building Fund, and also Of the St. James' Churchwar- dens' Additional Expenses Fund, a sale of work was held in St. James' School, Latchford, on Thursday, when the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Firth, presided over the opening ceremony, which was performed by Mrs. Broadbent. The tastefully arranged stalls were in the able hands of the following ladies : Congregational Stall.—Mesdames Dickson, Davies, Carruthers, Parry, Harris, Bell, Ingham and Tetlock. _ _

In his opening remarks the Vicar referred to the fact that it was Guy Fawkes' Day, and said that 300 years ago a tremendous plot, which had been hatched for the purpose of doing a great deal of harm, was frustrated. To-day the coun- try was in the presence of another great danger. A plot had been prepared by which a mighty blow was to bs struck at the British Empire; but they believed that to-day the hearts of their young men were as brave and strong as were those of the young men of 300 years ago. There had been a magnificent response to the call of duty, and from their own parish 250 men had gone to the front. (Applause.) They believed that God, who preserved them in 1605, would be with them in 1914, and that they had no cause to be afraid.
