div.p: 61111 H. MAltkUAib. DEN'

THE ONLY THING THAT COUNTS. All continues to go well at the front. In the west the Allies continue to hold the enemy in an iron grip, and another failure is being added to the KAISER'S programme. The road to Calais from Belgium is being strewn with the dead of the youth of the country, WILLIAM 11. pretends to rule, but which he has betrayed into an act of national suicide. Whether by chance or design is immaterial, but the British Army finds itself directly across the KAISER'S path again. When he was rolling away so light-heartedly for Paris it was FRENCH'S contemptible little Army that retired before his hordes, anti, in retir- ing, took the edge off his sword in such a manner that it stubbornly refuses to be ground again. The British Army has now been spirited away from the Aisne, and is on the direct path of the KAISER to Calais, which " must be taken at all costs." As before, FRENCH'S con- temptible little Army has exacted the full cost, but again the KAISER goes empty away. How severe the German losses have been in the last week or two, during which fresh armies have been brought up to hack their way through, the official dispatches have recently told us. We have not only learnt of their losses, but of the kind of men that have been opposed to us. Certainly it seems as though the Ger- man supply of first-class mends getting short, when, at the most critical point of the campaign, they employ such troops as those who have been heroic- ally, but in vain, hurling themselves at our men. "Certainly," says our official chronicler, "the way their advance was conducted showed a lack of training and faults in leading which the almost superhuman bravery of the soldiers could not counter-balance. It was a holocaUst. The spectacle of these devoted men chanting a national song as they marched on to certain death was inspiring. It was at the same time pitiable." Since then the same graphic pen has described the. "prodigious slaughter" we have inflicted upon the enemy, and—paradox of paradoxes in 20th century civilisation—all continues as, we say, to go well. But if we have inflicted tremendous punishment upon our adversaries we have ourselves, in company with our Allies, both French and Belgian, suf- fered grievous loss. The same authority that tells us, first hand, of the way our Army has more than main- tained-the glorious traditions to which it is heir, also tells us that final victory will rest with the side that can the longer bring up and "fling fresh forces into the fray." Are we prepared to say that Britain will be the one that shall bring up the last, and, consequently, struggle for national, nay, for domes-

div.head: IR, SATURDAYS NOVEMBER 7, 1914
div.p: IR, SATURDAYS NOVEMBER 7, 1914
tic, existence? That is the only thing
that matters for us all now. The war
so far as Germany is concerned has
degenerated into a war of hatred
against us, the English.
The lunatic
EMPEROR and his unscrupulous, mur-

deririg confederates, who, for the sake- of euphony, are called militarists, have educated the German people, by some Mysterious system of hypnotism, to look forward to "The Day" When they will enter into our heritage as a colon- ising and Imperial Power. They see "The Day" being indefinitely post- poned through the smashiqg that their culture-machine is•receivit*, largely at our hands, and their feelings are find- ing relief in "hymns of hate," directed against us specially, productions such as have never before disgraced even the days of a bitter war. If the Germans win, by any lack of foresight on our part, or failure to fling those final effec- tive forces into the fray through our taking success too much for granted, we may be sure that a worse fate than that which has befallen Belgium will befall this fair land of ours. For Bel- gium they professed friendship ; for us they declare unbridled and undying hatred. Where friends were ground to death, as Belgium was ground, what treatment shall be in store for deadly enemies? But we do not fear. , The young men of Great Britain only need to know that they are wanted, and the numbers that KITCHENER calls for will be at hand. They must come now, however. Now, when the battle can be fought in Europe. It would be criminal to wait until the Huns are knocking at the gates of our own cities. .The more we keep them in anxiety about their precious Rhine, the less time they will have to waste brooding over a raid upon our shores. We should be doing less than our duty did we not advise every young man of proper physique, whose chief and perhaps only responsibility is to the land which gave him birth and stands in urgent need of his services, to offer himself at the earliest moment. Since. the .war began no fewer than 7,000 men have enlisted for KITCHENER'S Army in this district. Of these, 2,26-4 were Warrington Men, a gre.al figure, seeing that al our large works, turning out Government orders, are employed thousands of men who are helping to defeat the foe just as much as if they had joined the Army. The men who are joining are not the same class as that to which the young recruit usually belongs. They are older, better devel- oped, determined men, who join for the set purpose of doing all they can, individually, to end this particular war in the right way for Britain. They do not drink, but their conduct in camp and their spirit "are all that can be desired. There is very little crime, and the keenness of all ranks is a plea- sure to watch. The officers live among the men and share all their labours. The men have enlisted to fight, and are tigers for work. They all want to learn, and whether it is drill, or mus- ketry, or lectures, the attention is main- tained. The good class of the men enables them to master their lessons much quicker than in the case of the ordinary recruits." That is the report we get of our four new Armies that will soon be ready to settle accounts with the KAISER. The difference between this material and the German material that we have been slaughter- ing "in columns," to quote the official message, is the difference that Sexists between conscript troops and those who gO into the fray because they feel the call from GOD no less than from KING. It is the difference that accounted for CAVOUR'S generous description of the British race in 1855. Said the great Italian statesman "England always began i with forces "inferior to her real means of action. "But disasters and defeats, instead of "shaking her confidence, have never "failed to encourage her to make new "efforts and new sacrifices. While "her enemies after some successes felt "their courage sink and their force "diminish, she grew in strength and "in means of action in proportion as "the war was prolonged." We hope we are still true to pattern, and that the boom which will now take place in recruiting will show the world that the heart of the nation that stands for freedom, for liberty, and for right, is still sound enough to impel the sons of that nation to respond once again in sufficient numbers to the call of duty.

div.head: TIIE HARVEST MOON.
div.p: TIIE HARVEST MOON.

What Last thou brought, 0 harvest moon, Climbing the eastern sky? What hast thou brought to our English fields, Where the peaceful hamlets lie? "Oh, I have brought fair fruits and flowers, Born of the long, bright summer hours, Songs of joy round the loaded wain, Bearing the stores of golden grain; Up from the fields the labourers come, And the harvest of peace is gathered home." What hast thou seen, 0 harvest moon, Over the northern wave? Our gallant sons go forth to war, The bravest among the brave. "Oh, I have seen your heroes go, With death around, above, below, Sailing beneath the eastern skies. The light of battle in their eyes; But over the seas the great ships come, And the harvest of death is gathered home." What hest thou seen, 0 harvest moon, Out on the eastern plain? The trenches are red with our brothers' blood, And strewn with the gallant slain. "What I have seen no tongue can tell, The battle-field is the mouth of hell! Slaughter and rapine, fire and sword, Are these Thy ministers, 0 Lord? But over the field God's angels come, And the harvest of war is gathered home." How long, how long, 0 harvest moon, Ere the strife and carnage cease? How long, how long, must we wait and pray For the dawn of love and peace? "0 the moons will rise and wax and wane Over the fields of the gallant slain; And long will the guardian angels go To succour the souls of friend and foe; But the day of the Lord will surely come, And Freedom's harvest be gathered home."
ALF= COUNLY.

div.head: DRINK IN WAR TIME.
div.p: DRINK IN WAR TIME.
Demand for Hestrioted Hours of " Opening."

div.head: REAL QUESTION AT ISSUE.
div.p: THE REAL QUESTION AT ISSUE.

There is a strong and growing feeling in town that the licensing justices have dismissed the question of the earlier closing of public-houses in Warrington rather too hurriedly. Another effort may be made to get them to reconsider the position with a view to taking action on a line with other places, especially recruiting centres. _

upon the taverns of this country, and men ques- tion, as never before, the social and economic value of them. The feeling is evidently abroad that they should be patronised as little as pos- sible, representing, as they do to a large extent, national and individual luxury and waste." I am sorry the magistrates have refused to put the Act into force, as I believe it was passed as a preventative measure, and not to be dormant until our statistics for drunkenness are higher than they were before the war.—Yours, 'BENJ. T. PARKES.
8, Willis-street, November 4, 1914.

WILL "THE TRADE" ACT? To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—l should think that after the latest appeal by Lord Kitchener, all concerned in the efficiency of the men who are being trained in our town, and who may shortly be called to take their place at the front, must be astounded at the stupidity of the Trade in turning a deaf ear to the obvious import of that appeal, which we are pleased to note has been very wisely and promptly responded to by the Trade in other towns. Is not the Trade in Warrington, which usually boasts itself of its patriotism, creating in the minds of the best citizens of the town on this occasion the impression that pecuniary gain weighs heavier than patriotism, and is more important to them than military efficiency, which Lord Kitchener wishes us to realise is the most urgent need of the hour? No such drastic measure is proposed in this country that has been carried into effect by the Czar of Russia, in prohibiting the sale of all in- toxicants throughout his vast dominions during the war, but simply a shortening of the hours of sale, opening at 9 a.m. and closing at 10 p.m., and refusing to serve women until 12 o'clock at noon. The erroneous impression seems to obtain that the special powers of the Chief Constable should only be exercised when there is an increase of drunkenness. I believe that this is an abso- lutely inverted view to take of the Act. It is rather to be applied to prevent an increase of drunkenness. The Trade has still its chance of falling into line with such places as Birkenhead and other towns we might mention. If they delay, I be- lieve Parliament will be compelled in the im- mediate future to invest other authorities with power to deal with this urgent question promptly and effectually.—Yours, &c., . CITIZEN.

UNDOING KITCHENER'S WORK. To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—ln opening my " Eiaminer "on Satur- day I was very pleased to see a letter from one of your lady readers in reference to the peti- tion for the early closing of public-houses. I think with her that "The Trade" is undoing the good work of Lord Kitchener, who asks us to keep temptation from our soldiers, so they will be fit and well. I myself have seen soldiers going to the railway station in a drunken con- dition. 11 we are to be victorious in this con- flict we must have sobriety amongst our troops. I would like to call the attention of all tem- perance men in the town to the remarks of Councillor Broadhurst at the Council meeting on Tuesday night. "Workman Jim" has said Elome funny things in his time, but his remarks on Tuesday night were the limit. He is allied with a party who stands for "The Trade" and makes "The Trade" its politics.—Yours, &c., DISGUSTED.

THE FUNDAMENTAL THING. To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—With great interest I read the letter of Miss Tanner re "Early closing of public-houses" in your issue of last Saturday, and thoroughly agrbe with every word. It is a matter of vital importance to us as a nation, undergoing such trying circumstances as we are at present ex- periencing. The duty of each one of us, as citi- zens of a great Empire, is to endeavour to main- tain her supremacy at home, while our brave soldiers and sailors are fighting to uphold her freedom and liberty abroad. Let us do all that lies in our power to assist them in this present struggle. To do this we must necessarily abandon every source by which excitement of mind is caused, and the first and fundamental thing that presents itself to every free-thinking individual is the early closing, if not complete closing, of all licensed premises during the period of the crisis. Sooner or later we shall be bound to adopt this method, so why beat around the bush? I I was extremely surprised to lehrn the results of the "Early closing petition," presented to our local magistrates by over two thousand con- scientious citizens of Warrington, who have the genuine interests of Empire at heart, and who recognise that the promotion of temperance in our midst is the first and greatest step towards establishing unity in our nation. I appeal to every free-thinking member of this community, who desires the welfare of our nation. earnestly to consider this question in all seriousness and to fight strenuously to make the next effort prove successful.—Yours, PRO BONO PUBLIC°.

div.head: CRIMINAL WASTE.
div.p: CRIMINAL WASTE.

At the best, spending our money on drink is luxury. But at the worst, and at a time like this, such spending is almost criminal. Surely the authorities will be wise in time, and help the people to save the money by reducing their temptations to spend it unwisely. By so doing the Government will conserve the national re- sources, increase the home industries of the country, and do much to lessen unemployment. They will maintain with far greater success a standard of health among the people by check- ing this drink waste; and by curtailing the hours of selling that which at the best is a luxury. . _ _ _ _
The safety of the Empire largely depends upon a sober people and a proper conservation a their resources.
PROTECT THE ARMY.

The Russians have sacrificed a revenue from the sale of spirits of £80,000,000 per annum. The immediate result has been shown by an unprecedented decrease in the criminal returns, an incontestable growth in the productivity of labour, and a large increase in savings bank deposits. Lord Roberts has said: "Give me a teetotal army, and j will lead it anywhere."

Admiral , Sir J. R. Jellicoe, Commander-in- Chief of the Fleet, said: "As regards straight shooting, it is everyone's experience that absti- nence is necessary for the highest efficiency." Sir Thomas Barlow, one of the King's physi- cians, in an address to all men serving the Empire, points out the disastrous effects of alcohol.

div.head: RECHABITES AND CLOSING TIME. ,Protest Against Decision of Licensing
div.p: THE RECHABITES AND CLOSING TIME. ,Protest Against Decision of Licensing
Justices.

At the quarterly meeting of the Warringtbn District of the Independent Order of Rechabites, held at Padgate last Saturday, Bro. D. R. Barker in the chair, it was decided to support by every available means Lord Kitchener's appeal to the public to abstain from offering drink to soldiers, a mistaken kindness which can only tend to make them unfit to perform their duty to the Empire at this critical junc- ture.

The meeting unanimously decided to protest against the decision of the magistrates to keep open the public-houses and other licensed prem- ises during the usual hours•at the present time, and instructed the secretary to send the follow- ing resolution tb the Press : „ _ .

_ "-`l'hat this meeting, comprising over 2,600 adult members, expresses its keen disappoint- ment at the decision of the magistrates declin- ing to take steps, as they were memorialised to do, respecting the curtailment of the hours for the sale of intoxicating liquors; and, in view of the example already set by many authorities in various parts of the country, and of the stupen- dous sacrifice made by and the urgent appeal made this week by Lord Kitchener, it sincerely hopes that further consideration will be given to this matter at a very early date."

div.head: WISH OF THE NAVAL AND MILITARY AUTHORITIES. To the Editor of "The Examiner."
div.p: WISH OF THE NAVAL AND MILITARY AUTHORITIES. To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—Will you please allow me an opportunity through your columns to save an erroneous im- pression being fixed upon the minds of your readers from the remarks of Councillor Broad- hurst? The Intoxicating Liquor (Temporary Restriction) Act, 1914, was introduced and pressed upon the House of Commons at the re- quest of the Naval and Military Authorities, and not, as Councillor Broadhurst suggests in his remarks, by the Temperance party. The Act was passed on Monday. August 31st, yet in Warrington no notice was taken of it up to September 15, and on that date the Citizens' Temperance League asked the Rev. T. T. James to interview the Revs. Canon Willis and Father Wilson, so that steps might be taken for a peti- tion to be signed at the various churches and forwarded to the authorities, asking them to put the Act into operation in Warrington—as it has been done in many districts, and there has been no panic.

Councillor Broadhurst on one occasion in Parr Hall had so much confidence in the people assembled that he cried "Stop the beer," "Stop the beer," but when our nation is in danger, and the Naval and Military Authorities appeal for help, that men may be efficiently trained to defend their country, he congratu- lates those who refuse to help them by respond- ing to the appeal, even after our distinguished Secretary of State for War, Lord Kitchener, appeals for sober soldiers. The "Brewers' Gazette," September 10, 1914, speaks differently, for it says: "It can hardly be wondered, then, if glances begin to be cast

div.head: CLEANEST SOLDIER.
div.p: THE CLEANEST SOLDIER.
Our Men Backed Against "Dirty TROOPS WHO APPRECIATE SOAP.

A few weeks ago we announced that Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons had sent half a mil- lion free tablets of "Good Luck" Soap to our soldiers at the front. The soap has arrived safely and the firm have already received many letters of thanks and appreciation of the gift. Captain Barker, writing on behalf of the officers and men of the Fifth Division, says:— "I can't tell you how grateful everyone is; it was very urgently wanted. The men have been having a very hard time, and we are fight- ing up to the best traditions of the Army. Again very many thanks from everyone. Your splen- did gift bucks up the men, because they feel you in England appreciate their efforts."
Major Grierly, commanding 26th Heavy Bat- tery, HG. Artillery, writes :

„ "-I have great pleasure in conveying at their request the thanks of the men of the Battery under my (command' for the gift of 'Good Luck Soap, which was received safely yester- day” -(October 27th). Lieutenant-Colonel Burnett, 18th Hussars, writes a similar letter, sayihg the soap was "most welcome" and "we are all greatly obliged to you for your kindly forethought."

div.head: OUR HEALTHY ARMY.
div.p: OUR HEALTHY ARMY.

Among the 600,000 under arms in the United Kingdom only five eases of typhoid fever were notified in the week ending September 26th, and ten in the week ending October 10th. These satisfactory figures were supplied by Sir J. Crichton-Browne, speaking on Saturday at the Caxton Hall meeting of the Sanitary Inspectors' Association. With proper precautions, he added, typhoid fever, that devastator of armies in the past, need not be feared, but typhoid was still a serious menace, and it was to be hoped that the use of anti-typhoid vaccine would be pressed upon our troops. He understood the wastage due to sickness had so far been exceptionally small. A well- versed Italian correspondent, who had visited all the arinie,s in the field, had declared that the British soldier was "undoubtedly the best fed, the cleanest And the healthiest in the field." With cleanliness—moral and physical—in their favour, we should have no misgivings as to the final success of our men over the dirty and demoralised, however courageous, millions opposed to them. Cholera was raging among the Austrian troops, and it was satisfactory to know that we had an apparently effective vaccine against that disease. It was used by the Greek Army in the Balkan War, and not a single case of cholera occurred.

div.head: GAS PROFITS.
div.p: GAS PROFITS.

Should Rates or Consumers Benefit? Judging from a discussion which has taken place in the Town Council, a very old problem in connection with municipal gas undertakings has cropped up in rather an acute form at Warrington. It will be seen from our -news columns that the point arose on the report of the District Auditor, in which various figures relating to the past year's working of the de- partment were drawn attention to. Among these was the large unappropriated balance, which the Auditor remarked seemed to be more than was necessary for a working balance., This item was also criticised by a member of the Council, but, apparently from not altogether the same standpoint; for he remarked that the balance appeared to have been used for one object only—to draw on from time to time to subsidise the rates. Some effects of the policy, as the matter strikes him, were indicated by the Councillor; and an excellent opening (of which he took full advantage) was afforded the Chairman of the Committee to "point a moral" without "adorning a tale." His view is that which is taken far more often by chairmen of Gas Committees than by those of Finance Com— mittees—" that the Gas Committee should no longer be a committee to bolster up the rates of the town "—and one can only hope that he at least succeeded in getting the Council as a whole to share his opinion. If, as was averred, the question for a long time lias been, "How much can we get out of the Gas Committee?' a principle has been adopted which is not the best possible in the interests of the undertak- ing.. Indeed, that the needs of the Gas Works have unavoidably to some extent been made subservient to the exigencies of the Finance Committee is a natural conclusion to be drawn from the statement that, when the profits of the department fell off, and the Finance Com- mittee asked for a certain sum for the relief (if the rates, the Gas Committee thought they would best spare it from an amount set aside for renewals to the gas-holders. As a matter of fact, with profit of some „tB,OOO, a sum of £11,500 has been handed over in relief of the rates. It would be far better, not only for the managers, but for the undertaking, for the consumers, and, also, no doubt, for the citizens generally, if the Councillors would only realise the soundness of the contention of the Chairman of the Gas Committee, that "they ought to make the gas cheaply for the consumers, and let the manager have the benefit of manufactur- ing and selling it cheaply." What is given to the rates must go on to the Price of gas.— Journal of Gas Lighting and Water Supply."

[Our contemporary is in error in its reference to the Chairman of the Gas Committee. It was Alderman Tinnion who spoke as a mem- ber of the committee; Alderman Pierpoint, who is chairman, did not speak.—ED.]

At the Borough Police Couri. on Thursday morning Patrick Hogan, 3, Howley-lane, War- rington, was charged with being drunk and disorderlly. in Bridge-street on Wednesday.— P.C. Rowles said lie was, on point duty at Bridge Foot, when he saw the prisoner, who was very drunk, dancinm round Oliver Cromwell's statue. (Laughter.) °lmmediately after he threw a tumbler at the statue and then commenced to search for a stone. When he was taken into custody he became very violent. He was fined 10s. and costs.

"The Geography of the War." In order that students of European histprY, and also of the present war, may be in a better position to understand something of the move- ments of each nation's armies they must pos- sess some geographical knowledge of the dis- tricts in which the conflict is raging, and in order to satisfy this demand, the local branch of the Workers' Educational Association have commenced a series of short lectnres on the " Geography of the War," conducted by Miss Hubback, of Lymm. This class meets at Atkinson's Cafe each TuesdaY at 6 [MM, and should be attended by every person desircus of knowing accurately the bearing of the many movements in this Titanic struggle. Territorial's Funeral.

A large crowd gathered- at the Cemetery ;on Wednesday afternoorf to witness the funeral of the late Private Thomas Morris, whose home was at 44, General-street, and who died from pneumonia in the City Hospital, Edinburgh, last Friday night. The private, who was only 23 years of age, belonged to "D" Company of the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, which lie joined three years ago. The Rev. T. Vickers conducted the service in the Cemetery Chapel, afterwards officiating at the graveside. The widow of the deceased and many relatives attended the funeral, And about 150 of the South Lancashires were also present. A firing party fired three volleys over the open grave and buglers sounded the "Last Post" at the conclusion of the ceremony, after which ma,ny beautiful floral tributes were laid on the grave.

Warrington Photographic Society. At the weekly meeting on Tuesday Mr. W. H. Hartley gave a very fine lecture, illustrated by lantern views, on " Belgium and Switzerland: Their !People and Towns." The first part, dealing with our Allies in the war, was most appreciated, the pictures of Brussels, Bruges and Antwerp eliciting the enthusiastic inter4st of the audience, which, by the way, was the largest so far this session. The scenes in the Ardennes were very fine, showing, as they did, agricultural methods so different from those of Southern Britain. Photographs of Basle were followed by wonderfully clear and fascinating pictures of the Alps, the rivers and the lakes, those of Lake Geneva being specially fine. The concluding section of the lecture was illustrated by many charming views of Zermatt and the country round the Matterhorn. The lecturer was heartily thanked and applauded at the close. Old English Fair Profits Allocated. The results of this year's Old English Fair were announced at a meeting held on Friday last, Mr. J. H. Smethurst presiding. The total cash received, including that from the draw, amounted to £1,532 Hs. 10d., and thekcost of production totalled £772 10s. 4d. The profit therefore reached the handsome sum of £760 Os. 61. This money has been allocated as fol- lows :—.e600 to the Infirmary current account; ,t 25 to provide a cot in the Infirmary for the Children's Ward; £lO to the Infirmary Special War Fund; £lOO to the Warrington and District Nursing Association; .£l.O to the Children's Summer Camp; £.lO to the St. John Ambulance; ..t.5 to Cripples' Guild.—A comprehensive vote of thanks was passed to the following :—The ladies and gentlemen who assisted at the Fair; the District Bank, for banking facilities, and for the staff at the cash office; various firms and the Corporation for assisting by the loan of materials and for cartage; Messrs. Caldwell, for assisting in the sale of tickets for the draw; firms who exhibited the prizes for the draw; and to Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, for fitting up the bar.—A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the business. St. John's Presbyterian Church: Diamond Jubilee Celebrations.

As will be seen from our advertising columns, a special season of Diamond Jubilee celebration in connection with the above church commences to-morrow, when the Very Rev. Ex-Moderator Dr. Monro Gibson will occupy the pulpit morn- ing and evening. This is not the sixtieth anniversary ,of the life of Presbyterianism in Warrington, or even of that pf the congregation of St. John's—in fact, an illustrated booklet has just been published, and may be had at the price of is. from the Minister (the Rev. Wm. Reid), which links Up the Presbyterianism of to-day with that which was in existence in the Cromwellian and Stuart times—but it is the Diamond Jubilee of the modern revival of the Church holding the Presbyterian Order in our midst. _ -

It is gratifying to realise that St. John's ap- pears tp have discovered the secret of rejuven- escence, and that never during its long history of struggle and conflict has the Presbyterian Church in Warrington possessed a spirit more youthful than to-day. In Dr. Gibson it welcomes a veteran who throughout his long life has been a constant and unwavering fighter on the side of truth in a hundred aspects, and who, like the congrega- tion to which he will minister to-morrow, has retained a heart young beyond the ordinary. A native of Whithorn, in the County of Wigtown, he entered upon his first charge just fifty years ago in Erskine Church, Montreal. Afterwards he became the minister of the Second Presby- terian Church, Chicago, and in 1880 came to St. John's Wood, London, where he ministered until last year. Dr. Gibson was called to the .Moderator's chair by the Synod in 1891. It is quite a number of years since Warrington last heard his ringing voice and plear enunciation, and on that occasion, if we mistake not, the Parr Hall was engaged. Many of those who then heard him will doubtless try and find a seat in the comparatively limited accommoda- tion which St. John's offers, and we bespeak for the venerable cleric a crowded. kirk.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1914.
Temperance Meeting. A public meeting under the auspices of the Warrington Band of Hope Union will be held to-morrow (Temperance Sunday), in the Co- operative Hall. Mrs. James Dodds will preside.
"Christianity and the War." Mr. IL J. Long, of Leeds, will give an address on the above subject at the Friends' Meeting House, Buttermarket-street, to-morrow. For Footballers. - - -
A special " Football Service" will be held in connection with the Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood to-morrow afternoon, when Councillor E. Osborne will preside.
Mr. Ziba Armitage. We are glad to learn that the latest news from Preston Brook is that Mr. Ziba Armitage has considerably improved in health during the last few days.

div.head: 1.8.5. A. Lecture.
div.p: 1.8.5. A. Lecture.
"The End of the Gentile Times: When?" is the title of a lecture to be given in the Park Picture Palace at 6.30 on Sunday evening. All seats will be free.

div.head: Mission Services.
div.p: Mission Services.
The Rev. R. Wood-Samuel, of the Chapel Royal, Savoy, London, will conduct special mis- sion services at St. Paul's Church to-day and on Sunday and Monday.

' Accident to Mr. George Dakin. Mr. George Dakin, who had been attending a meeting at the Infirmary, slipped down several steps as he was leaving the Institution yester- day and lacerated his scalp. He was detained as an in-patient, and is progressing favourably. To Insured Persons.

The Warrington Ingurance Committee give notice that insured persons desirous of changing their panel doctor, or institution, at the close of the current year, must acquaint the Clerk to the Insurance Committee (Mr. Alfred Tilling) with the fact not later than December Ist.

• Catholic Party and Dance. The.annual tea party and dance in aid of St. Mary's School, Warrington, was held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening, when about 400 spent a pleasant time. The League of the Cross Band was in attendance. Messrs. Henry Houghton, James Magrath and John Eckersley acted as M.C.'s! and Mr. A. Kilburn carried out the secretarial duties.

Mayoress's Concert to Dependents. The Mayoress has arranged a concert to be given in Parr Hall next Wednesday evening to the wives and other dependents of local soldiers and sailors. All entitled to attend are cordially invited. Tickets may be obtained at Parr Hall on Monday, Tuesday and Wednes- day, between 10 and 12 o'clock. For outside friends there will be a few seats at 6d. each.

Mayor and Mayoress "At Home." The Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peacock) will be "At Home" at the Municipal Museum from 3 to 5 and 7 to 8.30 on Thursday, November 19th. Those attending are remindell that this year the Cinderella Club has ceased its operations, and that in consequence gifts of toys and dressed dolls for the poor children of Warrington will be much appreciate.] Death of Mr. Samuel Bail

We regret to announce the death of -Mr. Samuel Ball (forinerly of Warrington and father of Mr. James Ball), which occurred at Manor, Saskatchewan, on October 13th. Mr. Ball, who was 80 years of age, was formerly a stocktaker for the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., and worked for that firm for about 27 years. With his wife and five mem- bers of his family, Mr. Ball left England•for Canada in 1892, and took up farming and stock raising. He sold ont " about five years ago and had since retired.

div.head: "A Naughty Girl."
div.p: "A Naughty Girl."

Announcing that by—a Majority of the Bench the case against her would be dismissed, the Mayor, at the Police Court yesterday, told Teresa Goddard, a domestic servant, employed by Mr. Sangster at the Royal Oak Hotel, Bridge- street, that she was a naughty girl. Teresa was charged with stealing a ring, valued at 305., the property of Nellie Bannister, a felloW-servant at the hotel. When she was taxed with the theft by Detective-Sergeant Reddington, she got the ring from under a chest of drawers, her explanation being that although she knew where the ring was, she "thought she would let Nellie find it for herself."

div.head: Forge Worker's Death.
div.p: A Forge Worker's Death.

An inquest conducted by the Deputy-Coroner (Mr. F. A. Jones) was held at the Police Build- ings on Thursday afternoon concerning the death of John Starkie, a forge worker, who had been living at 56, Haydock-street.—The evidence showed that on October 27th, as Starkie was using a wheelbarrow, his foot kicked against some scrap-iron and he fell on to the handle. He continued work that day, but later he was compelled to be attended by a doctor. He died on Monday.—Dr. Law, senior resident house surgeon at the Infirmary, said that lie had made a post-mortem examina- tion and was convinced that death was due to pneumonia, and the accident had nothing to do with it.—A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was returned, and sympathy was expressed with the relatives.

• Death of Mrs. M. Osborne. We record with regret the death of Mrs. Osborne, wife of Mr. M. Osborne, who passed away at her residence, Knutsford-road. A paralytic seizure, which-came without warning, occurred on Wednesday week, and the end came peacefully on Monday afternoon. Mrs. Osborne, who had entered her 70th year, had won the respect of a wide circle of friends, and her re- moval will bring a sense of loss to many. The interment took place on Thursday afternoon at the Warrington Cemetery. The service at the chapel and graveside was conducted by the Rev. Hugh Williamson and the Rev. Thompson Derry read the lesson. Among the mourners were: Mr. M. Osborne (husband), Messrs. Geo. Harry and John Osborne (sons), Mrs. Dawson, Mrs. Minards and Miss Ruth Osborne (daugh- ters), Mr. Wilbert Dawson, Mr. E. Minards and Mrs. Harry Osborne. Messrs. J. Mounfield and Sons had charge of the funeral arrangements. Mayor's Day. A special meeting of the Town Council will be held at noon next Monday for the purpose of electing the Mayor and Deputy-Mayor for the ensuing year, and the transaction of various routine business. The first proposition that will be submitted to the members is as follows : " That Mr. Peter Peacock be, and is hereby, re-elected Mayor for the ensuing year, and until the acceptance of office by his successor." ' The members will -also be asked to fix the dates of next year's Council meetings, appoint , the committees and elect their representatives on various other administrative bodies.

A meeting of the Friendly Societies of the borough was held at the Town Hall on Thurs- day night, at which it was decided to attend Divine service with his Worship the Mapr on Sunday, November 15th. The order of the pro- cession will be advertised in our columns later. Mr. T. P. Bradshaw was asked to marshal the procession once again.

Wesleyan Prize Choir. The record audience which attended the Bold- street Wesleyan Prize Choir's annual concert, held on Thursday evening in the Schoolroom, had the privilege of listening to an excellent programme. Miss Bessie Dutton, who pre- sided, was introduced by the Rev. Hugh Wil- liamson (minister-in-charge) and had a hearty reception. In a brief address Miss Dutton said it was good for them to have some recreation at a time like this, if it was only to take their minds for a time from the terrible happenings on the Continent. Miss Dutton then paid a very high tribute to the work of the soldiers; she wished them God-speed. After speak- ing of the valuable work of the Wesleyan Choir, she referred in, complimentary terms to the services of the conductor, Mr. Frank Hickman, and Mrs. Booth, the ladies' trainer. (Applause) The programme, which included many stir- ring patriotic items, was then proceeded with, the artistes being as follows: Mrs. Booth, Misses M. Blackburne, B. Brough, D. Caine, Sophia Cross, Elsie Evans, C. Hanrey, N. Kershaw, Emily Taylor, and M. Whitmore; Messrs. J. Clayton, A. Greenhalgh, T. Mills, E. H. Pearce (whose song, " For King and country," was particularly appreciated), C. Ran-ling and W. Warburton. The choir also rendered several choruses of fine quality; and "Mrs. Murphy" (Mr. 11. M. Ashton) gave one of her celebrated, mirth-pro- voking addresses.
The-takings were on behalf of the local War Relief Fund and the Sunday School New Piano Fund. To the former a sum of rts will be contributed.

div.head: CALL TO ARMS.
div.p: CALL TO ARMS.
FROM WORKS TO BARRACKS.
About 30 men have enlisted from the War-
rington works this week. Messrs. Crosfield's accounted for 12 and Messrs. Rylands' for 6. BAPTIST MINISTER AS CHAPLAIN.
The Rev. T. N. Tattersall, of Kettering, a fellow-student with the Rev. H. Ogden, and the minister who officiated at the marriage of Mr. Ogden, has gone to the front as a chaplain.

div.head: COUNCILLOR WITH THE COLOURS.
div.p: A COUNCILLOR WITH THE COLOURS.

Councillor Furness explained at the meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council on Wednesday that it was necessary to appoint someone on the War Committee in place of Councillor Garnett, who had gone away with the colours. He suggested Dr. Murray, and the Council agreed to his aprintment. W.L.D. TRANSPORT . ANYI SUPPLY

div.head: COLUMN.
div.p: COLUMN.

A reserve of the -*e"-si.lancashire Division Transport and Supply Column is now being raised, and for the Divisional Train, horse drivers, wheelwrights, saddlers and farriers are required, and for the Divisional Supply Column motor lurry drivers and assistants, workshop staff, fitters and turners, blacksmiths, wheel- wrights, electricians, warehousemen and por- ters. The recruits' office is at 46, Legh-street.

C.L. BRIGADIERS WITH THE COLOURS. The headquarters staff of the Church Lads' Brigade are anxious to receive names of present and ex-members who are desirous of serving King and country. A special C.L.B. Battalion of the King's Royal Rifles is in training at Den- ham, and it is now proposed to form a second similar battalion, and those willing to join should communicate with the headquarters, Aldwych House, Catherine-street, Aldwych, London, W.C. The Chaplain-General, in recog- nition of the unique fact that the C.L.B. Bat- talion consists entirely of Churchmen, has de- tailed a whole-time chaplain to minister to its spiritual needs. It is a very interesting fact that hundreds of former C.L.B. members are amongst the Canadian troops which have re- cently landed in Europe to help the Mother Country. In addition, over one-third of the Newfoundland contingent, which is 500 strong, are keen ex-members of the brigade, whilst the commanding officer, Captain W. H. Franklin, sis limself a present C.L.B. officer.

div.head: " TOMMY'S " WIVES AND BAIRNS.
div.p: " TOMMY'S " WIVES AND BAIRNS.
Runcorn Guardians Favour Bigger Allowances.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, held at Dutton on Tues- day, Mr. Spruce presiding, the Berwick-on-Tweed Guardians asked the Board to support the fol- lowing resolution: "That this Board of Guar- dians strongly urges the Government to increase the pensions of our soldiers and sailors and the allowances made to the ,families of the men killed in action, and that more liberal allow- ances be made to the wives and children, and the mothers and sisters of those incapacitated, and of dependents, along the lines of the Work- men's Compensation Act."

Mr. Morris: I move that we give that our hearty support. Mr. Wright: I second. Mr. Hallows supported, remarking: We don't want the sailors and soldiers in the future to be in the Workhouses, or begging for bread." (Hear, hear.) Mr. Roylance mentioned the case of the wife of a teamsman, whose husband received 245. and a house in ordinary times, and who was getting 325. per week whilst her husband was at the front..

The Chairman: That is an exception. Mr. Morris: How much do the soldiers get per day? Mr. Jones: We are dealing with what the dependents get when a soldier is killed. To give them, say, ss. per week is a scandal. Mr. Lister-Kaye: We ought to do anything we can to support the proposal to give these dependents „t 1 or .t 1 10s, per week. It was decided to accord support to the reso- lution.

div.head: POOR LAW OFFICERS AT THE FRONT.
div.p: POOR LAW OFFICERS AT THE FRONT.

What a Guardian Wanted to Know. At their meeting on Wednesday the Warring- ton Board of Guardians were asked by the Ber- wick-on-Tweed Union to support the following resolution: " That this Board of Guardians strongly urges the Government to increase the pensions of our soldiers and sailors and the allowances made to families of men killed in action, and that more liberal allowances be made to the wives and children and mothers and sisters of those incapacitated, and of dependents, along the lines of the Workmen's Compensation Act." Mr. Brooks: I think the Government have enough on their hands without a resolution of that kind. I move that we take no notice of the letter.

The members agreed. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: On this point I would ask how many of our officials have gone from the House in order to join the Army, and under what conditions they have gone? The Clerk: One of the attendants has been called up, and the assistant master volunteered for_Kitchener's Army,

Mr. Mather: And the Chaplain. Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Under what conditions have they gone as regards the House? Is it full pay whilst away? The Chairman: No. Mr. Mather: One of the chaplains is a major and the other a captain.

div.head: KNUTSFORD DIVISION LIBERALS' SUGGESTED MINIMUM.
div.p: KNUTSFORD DIVISION LIBERALS' SUGGESTED MINIMUM.

The Knutsford Division Liberal Assoc:ation have forwarded the following resolution passed at an executive meeting to the Prime Minister, the First Lord of the Admiralty, and Lord Kitchener "That the Executive of the Knutsford Divi- sion Liberal Association strongly urges on the Government that the minimum allowances and pensions should be as follows: " „21 a week for the widow or for the mother dependent of every soldier and sailor killed. "£1 a week for the wife of every soldier and sailor engaged in fighting, and 2s. 6d. for each child. "i 1 a week for every soldier and sailor per- manently maimed by fighting."

SALVATION ARMY AMBULANCES. The Salvation Army is raising a sum of £2,000 for the purchase of five specially built and pro- perly equipped ambulance motors, which shall constantly operate between the firing line and the bases, and shall be manned by Salvation- ists. In order to help on the project, the local S.A. Band have contributed 6 guineas from their fund, and this afternoon and evening they will play in the streets and to-morrow evening in the Army Hall, in aid of the scheme, dona- tions being invited from the public.

div.head: FOR "THOSE HE'S LEFT BEHIND."
div.p: FOR "THOSE HE'S LEFT BEHIND."

This week relief has beenafforded' in about 1,000 Warrington cases by the Soldiers' and Sailors' Association, whose local office is at the Parr Hall. Altogether, over .t 1,400 has now been paid out locally in relief.

div.head: RASH ON sAsY'S FAtiA AND HEAD
div.p: RASH ON sAsY'S FAtiA AND HEAD

9, Nelson-terrace, City-road, London, N., Bug.—" My baby, while cutting her teeth, came out in a rash on her face and head. The irrita- tion caused her to rub it and it made it break out in running sores. Though only a baby seven months old, and having her hands in gloves day and night, she would rub it until she was a sight with blood. At night she seemed worse for she would lie and moan as though in pain all through the night. "They said my baby had eczema and gave me some ointment, but it got worse, completely covering her head and face. Nothing seemed to stop the irritation so she could get a little sleep. After trying all I could and getting no sleep for two months, finding it still getting worse and breaking out on the body, I gave up all hope. Then I sent for a sample of Cuticura Soap and Ointment and the first application gave, baby instant relief, for she went to sleep for a good two hours. We purchased more. My baby improved wonderfully and at the end of six weeks she did not have a sore on her. She has not a sign of eczema." (Signed) Mrs. G. Reynolds, Jan. 21, 1914. Although Cuticura Soap and Ointment are sold by chemists throughout the world, a sample of each with 32-p. Skin Book will be sent•post free upon re- quest. Address post card: P. Newbery and Sons, 27, Charterhouse-square, London, E.C.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
FINE PLAY AT•THE ROYAL COURT.

" The Story of the Rosary "—a romantic play which makes an irresistible appeal—is drawing crowded houses twice nightly at the Royal Court Theatre this week. It is not, as the title might suggest, a dramatised version of Mrs. Barclay's famous novel. From the pen of Mr. Walter Howard, who gave to playgoers " The Midnight Wedding," "The Prince and pie Beggar Maid," and other sterling successes, it holds the emotions from beginning to end. It concerns the love of a young officer who marries his sweetheart-in the little convent church the night before his regiment marcnes to war, and leaves her at the church door in the care of a dear old priest. As a talisman she places her rosary round his neck as he leaves her. After many months of sorrow and persecution, of hope deferred and resignation to the fact of his death, the young otHer wins through and brings the rosary back to his bride in the old priest's garden. It is a charming story, charmingly told, and the extraordinary success which has greeted the play wherever it has been staged has been thoroughly deserved. Mr. R. Scrope Quentin plays the part of the hero, Paul Romain, in just the right spirit, never lacking fire in the more strenuous pas- , sages, and touching just the right note of ' sentiment in the tender scenes with his lady fair. Miss Evelyn Carleton plays up to him splendidly as the heroine, Venetia &bran, rising to great heights in the big scene of the play, in which she hears tidings of Paul's sup- posed death, but, failing to grasp the meaning of the news, goes on joyously preparing against his homecoming with his regiment. It is a fine scene finely played and gets a rare grip of the audience. Mr. George E. Butler, with a naturalness which adds to the effectiveness of his acting, gives a clever reading of the part of the villain, Phillip Romain, and Mr. Cyril Austen-Lee stands out conspicuously for his treatment of the part of "Karl Larose-," the man who, from bad beginnings, "makes good" in a manner which touches the hearts of all. Mr. George Barran, as Coronet Hildebrand, handles an important part most capably, and Mr. J. W. Evelyn gives a sympathetic reading of the role of the venerable Father Theodore; whilst Miss Dulcie Lawrence gets in some Most effective work as the loving and lovable Mother Superior. As Lieutenant Peterkin, Mr. Leslie Hamilton supplies that fighter vein which is so necessary to the complete success of a modern melodrama, Miss Ruby Leyton, as Mina, and Mr. Arthur Byron, as Uncle Winkelstein, ren- dering him loyal assistance in his task of laughter-raising. 1" The Rosary" is well worth seeing.

div.head: An Old Favourite Next Week.
div.p: An Old Favourite Next Week.

Brought "-slap-bang up-to-date,"---t.hat old favourite, "The billy Slavey," one of /the merriest musical comedies on the road, will hold the boards at the Royal Court Theatre next week, when the cast will include Mr. W. T. Thompson as Roberts, a part played by him well over 2,000 times.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Even the most fastidious cannot fail to be pleased with the excellent programme provided at the Hippodrome this week, for it is full of first-rate turns. One of the most clever and daring cycle acts we have seen is presented by the Edievicta Troupe. These charming ladies Perform the most, intricate tricks with marvel- lous ease and rapidity, and a welcome feature ,about their show is that it is quite off the beaten track of ordinary cycle turns. The juvenile member of the troupe gains special applause on account of her faultless imitation of her elders. Mr. F. V. St. Clair rouses the greatest enthusiasm with his crisp and breezy war songs, "The Peace Congress," "Carving up the sausage," and "Follow the • drum." Copies of the last number are sold in the build- ing at twopence each, the proceeds being de- voted to the Prince of Wales' Fund. Mr. St. Clair is also successful with his recitation, "The house with the open door." Con and Conrad, in "An Exciting Time in the Yungle," are as popular as ever with their acrobatic eccentricities. The Burnetti Brothers are clever knockabout comedians and tumblers, who play the violin whilst posturing in all manner of difficult positions. "Bill's Last Chance" is the appropriate title of a clever comedy duo- logue presented by Miss Constantia Brookes and Mr. Knox Orde. Takase, the clever Japanese magician, pays a welcome return visit and gives his audiences "ten minutes of mystery." Jenny Robbins is a breezy comedienne and dancer, and Tim Carlisle pleases with his ditty, "I'm the bad lad of the family." Next Week's Attractions._

_ Next week's programme will include: Helena Millais and Company in the cowboy sketch, "Silver Creek"; Nora and Sidney Kellogg, musicians; Charlene and Charlene, drawing- room entertainers; .fi!.rtbur Royd, in patriotic songs; Felix and Fisher, comedy gymnasts; Little Doris, violinist; and Syd Aloorhouse.

div.head: gTAR KINENIA.
div.p: gTAR KINENIA.

The management of the Star Binema pre- sented a splendid programme at the beginning of the week and are following it up with an equally good one this week-end. The first pro- gramme included "The World and the Woman" and "The Chasm "—two splendid dramas, in which difficult problems were solved very hap- pily. "A Colonel in Chains" proved to be one of the most thrilling instalments of the fort- nightly serial, "The Adventures of Bathlyn." That favourite song, "Farewell, Isabelle," was illustrated with a series of beautifully coloured slides. The war films were a great attraction, including as they did recent issues of the " Gaumont Graphic" and" Pathe's Animated Journal." An instructive " special" which fol- lowed the latter was British Troops in France." " Caught in the Bain" was the title of a fine comedy. The second set of films, now shoving, should not be missed. It includes: "Shadows of a Great City," and a great war film, "The Evacu- ation of Ghent and Ostend."

div.head: Next Week.
div.p: Next Week.

Interesting programmes are promised for next week. On the first three nights "Antwerp Under Shot and Shell" and " Lily of the Val- ley" will form the chief attractions, whilst for the remainder of the week the principal film will be "In the Hands of London 'Crook.' "
WAR ITEMS.
_TEACHERS AND _SCHOLARS HELP.
The teachers and scholars of the Parochial Boys' School have contributed the sum of .210 towards the local Belgian War Refugees' Fund. PAROCHIAL SCHOOL ROLL OF HONOUR.I

_ An effort is being made to obtain the names of all old scholars of the Parochial Boys' School who are serving with the Army or Navy in the present war, the idea being to emblazon them on a roll of honour. WYCLIFFE MEN AT THE FRONT.

The current issue of the Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church Magazine contains the names of 34 members of the church who are now serving with the colours, and also the names of seven who have gone from the Elmwood-avenue Church.

div.head: PICTURE HOUSE.
div.p: PICTURE HOUSE.

Drama and comedy are well blended in•the programme which concludes to-night at the Picture House. The principal attraction is the two-reel drama, "His Country's Bidding," whilst the other dramas, "Little Senorita" and "The Clash of Virtues" are also very good. The comedy element is supplied by the films "The Heavenly Widow," "Bunny Buys a Hat" and "Tango Trouble." The Gaumont Graphic- series of the latest news in pictures is as inter- esting as ever.
Next Week.
Interesting programmes are promised for next week, when tile chief attractions win be pro- vided by the films "Hands •of Horror and "The House Discordant."

div.head: PICTUREDROME.
div.p: PICTUREDROME.

The programme submitted at the Picture- drome for the latter part of this week is of a very entertaining character. "A Queen's Love," a coloured drama in three parts, is the principal attraction, whilst other good films are "A Matrimonial Advertisement," " Mabel's Stormy Love Affair," and "The Vapour Bath," comedies; "A Little Shoe," drama; "The Alpine Road," scenic; and the always popular " Gaumont Journal."
Next Week. Typical Picturedrome programmes will be submitted next week, when the principal films will be "Victims of Blackmail" and "The Mysterious Shot."

BAPTISTS TO HELP BELGIANS. The members and congregation of the Baptist Church at Latchford have undertaken a most commendable enterprise, and one which de- serves to be imitated by other religious bodies, in furnishing a house and undertaking•to pro- vide for a family of Belgian refugees. The Corporation has granted the use of the house known as "Black Bear House" in Knutsford- road free of rent for the purpose, and the neces- sary preparations are already in hand. Messrs. E. Lloyd Jones and S. Fernley have charge of the collecting arrangements, and Nurse H. F. Smith has consented to act as matron of the home.

div.head: OFF ONE DUTY; ON ANOTHER!
div.p: OFF ONE DUTY; ON ANOTHER!

It was mentioned at the Warrington Rural District Council meeting on Wednesday that Mr. Newcombe (the surveyor) had been ordered to take several German prisoners from Sankey to Newbury in his motor car. Ile was away three days. MISSION MEMBERS' PRACTICAL SYMPATHY.

At a meeting of church members of the Working Men's Mission at Bank Quay on Sun- day it was decided that the Mission should accept responsibility for a Belgian family of five or six members. A house will be fourfd, probably within the neighbourhood of the Mis- sion, and the members present promised to find the necessary articles for furnishing it, and also promised to accept financial responsibility during the war.

div.head: MEN-111/NED IN. DISPATCHES.
div.p: MEN-111/NED IN. DISPATCHES.

Sergtr.:ll-1-a-jOi; Roberts,, who was -recently men- tioned in dispatches, and who, when on fur- lough, makes his home with his brother, Mr. A. Roberts, of 10, Amelia-street, Warrington, was in his boyhood a sergeant in the St. Elphin's (Warrington) Company of the Church Lads' Brigade. A son of the late Quartermas- ter-Sergeant Roberts, who was for several years stationed with the South Lancashire Regiment at Orford Barracks, he joined the 2nd Battalion of his father's regiment as a drummer, and, being rapidly promoted, received the coveted crown and stripes at the comparatively early age of 32.
VICAR OF ST. ANN'S AND THE BELGIANS

Announcing that he will be pleased to receive any additional contributions to the amount al- ready collected in St. Ann's Church for the Belgian Refugees' Fund, the Vicar (the Rev. James Davies) writes: "What our debt is to Belgium no one can fully tell. If there had been no Belgium check? What of France? What of dear old England? We owe the brave, bold, fearless Belgians very, very much. May God repay them their great sacrifices, and may we do our share in restoring to them their country, and re-building and re-fitting their homes, their hearths, their factories, and their farmsteads."

div.head: SCHOLARS AID WAR FUNDS.
div.p: SCHOLARS AID WAR FUNDS.

The scholars of the Municipal Secondary School continued their efforts on behalf of the war funds on Saturday afternoon, when an en- joyable social, arranged by the members of Form Va., was held. The scholars provided an abundance of refreshments, and arranged a series of dances, which were held in the base- ment of the school and thoroughly enjoyed by the 120 pupils who attended. Competitions also proved an interesting feature. Members of the school staff present were: Mr. E. S. A. Robson (head master), the Misses Jolley and Morris, and Messrs. Broome, Hoyle .and Marshall.
Asa result of this patriotic effort, over £3— the entire proceeds—*ill be distributed amongst the various relief funds.

SOLDIERS' RATIONS STOLEN. , • At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, Edward Kelly and Patrick Glynn, both of no fixed abode, were charged on remand with hav- ing been found on the enclosed premises of Orford Barracks for an unlawful purpose.—lt was stated that both men had been informed that a man for whom they were seeking was not at the barracks. They went round to the back of the premises and sat down at the dining table just when tea was about to be served. It was also pointed out that rations for about 30 men had been taken by men of prisoners' char- acter. Asked by Detective Summers why they went to the barracks, prisoners said they were hungry and wanted something to eat.--Kelly was sent to prison for one month, and Glynn, who had no previous record, was committed for seven days. "NOT FIT FOR A SOLDIER."

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, Joseph Mullen, of no fixed abode, was sent to prison for three months for having been found on the enclosed premises of Orford Barracks for an unlawful purpose.—Corporal Andrews said he found prisoner in his bedroom early one morning with his (the corporal's) trousers in his hand. Asked for his pass for the barracks, prisoner was unable to show one. Prisoner had been telling different people that he had to draw £lO from the barracks, but that was not so.— Detective-Sergeant Reddington said prisoner had been discharged from the Army as not being fit for a soldier.—Prisoner: Non compos mentis. (Laughter.) I came for my money.— When committed to prison, prisoner said "I would sooner go to the Assizes to be tried."— The Clerk: You cannot have the option. RADDON COURT HOSPITAL. The expenses incurred in getting thisJiospital ready have been considerable, and further help is urgently needed to carry on the good work that has already been begun. There are many willing helpers who are doing all they possibly can, and cannot be expected to do more, but it is felt that there must be amongst Warringtonians others who would help, and would do their share, if they were given a lead or knew in what direction they could best serve the interests of our country. All those who have not yet had an opportunity of helping will no doubt be glad to hear that it is proposed to hold a " Pound " Day on Thurs- day, the 12th inst., and on each second Thurs- day of the following months at Raddon Court, when parcels, no matter how large or small, ' containing groceries, bread, butter, tea, eggs, notepaper, Fze., will be most gladly accepted. PREPARATORY TRAINING CORPS' BUSY

div.head: AFTERNOON.
div.p: AFTERNOON.

The members of the Warrington and District Preparatory Training Corps have entered with zest upon the military training, which is, in case of need—and, after the filibustering exhibi- tion off Yarmouth, who can tell wh4n that need may arise?—to fit them to play a part in home defence. On Saturday afternoon, to the num- ber of nearly four hundred, they joined in a route march to Orford, setting out from the Town Hall, after parading on the lawn. They were under the command of Sergeant-Major Sullivan, and, as they marched, they were headed by the bugle band of the St. Paul's Company of the Church Lads' Brigade. On arrival at Orford they put in an hour's stiff drill. As they were returning to Warrington rain began to fall, and an open-air recruiting meeting which had been arranged in the joint interests of Kitchener's Army, the Warrington Territorials, and the Training Corps, had to be postponed until some more propitious day.

KILLED AT SOISSONS. Official intimation has been received in War- rington this week that Sergt. Arthur B. Praeger, of the 9th Lancers, was killed on October Ist, whilst in action at Soissons. The fifth and youngest son of the late Herr Praeger, the well- known Dutch linguist and musician, the de- ceased sergeant was only 29 years of age. After leaving the People's College he entered the em- ployriaent of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., quitting that firm 15 years ago in order to enlist. He was well known in local athletic circles as a footballer and poloist. When 17 years of age, the deceased sergeant was selected for, and played in, the final for the Cavalry Football Cup. He was captain of his regimental football team for nine years and captain of the hockey team for 10 years. He also played half-back for Margate for two seasons-1912 and 1913—his regiment being the stationed at Canterbury. In all, he held ii medals for football, polo, hockey, and long dis- tance running.

Only three years of his military career were served in this country, the remaining 12 being spent in India and South Africa. The deceased i stood nearly 6ft. n height, and was 131st. in weight. lie was not married, but he leaves a mother, three brothey6 and two sisters to mourn their less. lie was wounded twice previously to the fatal hit, viz., at Mons and Cambrai, and he took part in the famous charge at Cam- brai, when the 9th Lancers, under Captain _Grenfel, captured ten big German guns.

div.head: ON THE MONMOUTH.
div.p: ON THE MONMOUTH.

A Warringtonian who was Anxious to Get at the Enemy. At least one Warrin,gtonian was upon the cruiser Monmouth, viz., Able Seaman Joseph Hargreaves, the eldest son of Mr. George Har- greaves, of 15, Albert-terrace, Howley, who is in the employ of the Firth Company. Seaman Hargreaves had only been on the Mon- month since July, and his father had not seen . him since the beginning of the war. He heard from him, however, a fortnight ago—the first chance his son had had of writing. That letter told of coming trouble. It was despatched from Quabot, near Cape Horn, and said that the sailors were expecting a skirmish with the German cruisers, as they had heard they were in the district. The seaman, however, told his father not to worry, for he was quite all right, and all the "tars" were only too anxious to get at the enemy. Since receiving this communication, Mr. Hargreitves has had no tidings of his sailor son. Seaman Hargreaves is a fine, strapping, young fellow of 18. He joined the Royal Navy exactly two years ago, entering on boy's hating, and very soon was made petty officer boy. This position, however, he held only for a few months, for he was promoted to instructor boy, which position he retained for nine months. when, having reached the age of 18, he entered .on man's service, and was placed on the books of the Monmouth. ON THE GLASGOW. A Warringtonian in the person of Lance-Cor- poral Alfred Purcell. R.M.L.1., whose relatives now reside at 58, Whetstone-lane, Birkenhead, . was in the recent naval engagement in the „ Pacific. He is borne on the books of H.M.S. Glasgow. Prior to enlisting, the gallant lance- corporal was employed in the St. Helens Cable Company's works.

div.head: NEWS FROM THE FRONT.
div.p: NEWS FROM THE FRONT.

According to a correspondent of the "Central News" there are many foes which assail our gallant troops besides the enemy. "Of the injured and invalids I have seen," says tne writer, "it is remarkable to find a high pro- portion suffering from muscular rheumatism, an ailment which gives them more pangs than do bullet-wounds." This merely confirms the opinion of all who suffer from this painful and agonising ailment. No one at home or abroad is free from its ever-present danger, and during the damp and dismal days and nights which we are now having no one knows when he too may be stricken down by rheumatism in one or other of its varied forms.

div.head: LIBERAL WOMEN'S SUCCESSFUL EFFORT.
div.p: LIBERAL WOMEN'S SUCCESSFUL EFFORT.
Over £lO Raised for More Material.

To swell the coffers of the Liberal Women's Working Party, who are rendering such splen- did service in making comforts for the soldiers, a highly successful whist drive was held in the Crosfield Memorial Hall on Thursday evening. Admirable arrangements had been made by the organisers of the function, Mrs. E. A. Sanders and Mrs. Collin, and they were ably gssisted by Mesdames F. Davies, H. March, Hough, Percival, Pendlebury, and Miss E. Hough. Everything had been given voluntarily, includ- ing the refreshments, which were served at an interval, and the prizes. So large • was the attendance that in addition to the large room upstairs being used the lower room was also filled with interested players. After many skilfully played games the prize-winners were announced as follows :—Ladies: 1, Mrs. Locker; 2, Mrs. Savage; 3, Mrs. Knowles. Gentlemen: 1, Mr. Simpson; 2, Mr. Nurse; 3, Mr. Shaw. In the lower room the prizes were won by Mrs. Jeffery and Mr. T. A. Ward. In the course of a congratulatory speech, Mrs. Osborne thanked the ladies and gentlemen who had attended in such large numbers, and by so doing had helped to provide the committee with money to buy the necessary goods for mak- ing garments for the soldiers at the front. They had already done a splendid work and they wanted to continue it. The success of that 'function was due to Mrs. Sanders and Mrs. Collin for the excellent manner in which they had arranged everything. (Hear, hear.) Mr. F. Hallett, Councillor Barton and Mrs. Lindley were to be thanked for giving the prizes, as also were the Co-operative Society for lending the tables, and those who had given the refresh- ments. (Hear, hear.) The Mayoress then presented the prizes in a gracious manner, and on the proposition of Mr. Sanders she was accorded a hearty vote of thanks, as also was Mrs. Osborne. A sum of over .tlO was realised, and it will be spent in 'materials. GARMENTS FOR WOUNDED INDIANS. Mrs. Edelsten reports that the flow of cloth- ing continues unabated. There were again piles of garments to be seen on the tables at the Town Hall, and 368 articles were dispatched. Fazakerley Hospital had a large parcel, and a substantial sack went to Major Roger Willcocks for the use of the hospital ship Sicilia, which is conveying the wounded Indian troops to Eng- land. The mine sweepers and the Belgians at Alexandria Palace, Wood Green, were also not forgotten. Handsome contributions were received from. the Mayoress, Mrs. Allison, Mrs. Birtles, Mrs. Burleigh, Mrs. James Fairclough, Miss Gorse, the children of St. Luke's Sunday School, the children of the Sacred Heart School, the Women's Tariff Reform League, the Training College, and many others. Warm shirts and socks are still greatly needed.

UNIONIST WOMEN'S BUSY WEEK. The sewing party in connection with the Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform Leagues have been particularly busy this week, and have sent a large number of parcels to Warrington soldiers, both at home and abroad. div.p: No Compensation. Referring to a case of personal injury through dangerously-placed telegraph poles, the Chair- man of the Sankey Parish Council observed that the Government Telegraph Department could not give compensation "because they were not - legany entitled to do So." Of course not. 'Twas ever thus. The person who succeeded in obtain- ing compensation from a Government Depart- ment would be able to recover butter from a dog's throat and to extract blood from a stone. I don't believe there ain't no sich person—any more than there was a Mrs. Harris in Sairey Gamp's circle of acquaintance. In a town in which I once lived the postmaster was little better than an automaton bound with red tape. If an aggrieved one insisted upon seeing him in order at he might lay his complaint in per- son, the official would simply and without a word hand him or her a printed copy of the reguletions bearing upon the point raised, and nothing that the sufferer could urge by way of indignant protest and disgust would cause him to relax a muscle or turn a hair. A lady told me that an apologetic postman had handed to her a hopelessly crushed parcel of millinery, ad- mitting that he was ashamed to deliver it, and had said as much to his superior at the office. She had interviewed the wooden postmaster with' the usual result—a marked copy of the regulations showing that no claim for compensation would be entertained unless certain elaborate and prac- tically impossible precautions had been taken; impossible, because no milliner could ever be induced to comply with the conditions. The only alternative was to send the millinery by rail thereafter, for, if their servants are some- times careless in handling parcels entrusted to them, the companies are, as a rule, just and reasonable when loss and damage are proved against them, and do not systematically use their power to deprive the public of their rights. On the other hand, I never knew one obtain redress from any Government Department—and my experience is pretty extensive, for my father was in one at Somerset House a great many years.
A Common Offence.

So far from the railway companies taking un- due advantage of the public, the boot is gener- ally on the other foot. To travel by train with- out ticket and with the object of avoiding pay- ment of the fare is a favourite form of fraud, .and it is by no means ib.variably detected. The perpetrators appear to regard it as a venial offence, and some who get through undetected are apt to brag about their exploits, being ap- parently incapable of realising their con- temptible meanness. I once knew a young in- surance agent who repeatedly descended to trickery of this kind to save a penny fare, and when at last he was caught in the act it cost him in fine and costs—to say nothing of the ' humiliating exposure—much more than he had saved. However, by thereafter walking cir- cumspectly, he managed to regain confidence, and when last I heard of him he was an assist- ant superintendent for the same assurance com- pany in another town. Moreover, between the extremes indicated, there are cases detected which do not get into court. Years ago, in a dis- trict in which I was working at the time, two such actually occurred in the same family, one of the youthful offenders being a bank clerk, and somehow their father managed to persuade the company not to summon them before the magis- trates, although the offences were committed on widely different dates.

The Bridge Inscription. As I read Alderman Bennett's criticism of the proposed panel inscription for the new bridge, I was irresistibly reminded of the following : " When I look" (says Addison) "upon the tombs of the great, every emotion of envy dies within me. When I read the epitaphs of the leautiful, every inordinate desire goes out; when

JOTTINGS BY AN OLD II meet with the grief of parents upon a tomb- stone, my heart melts with compassion; when I see the tomb of the parents themselves. I con- JOURNALIST. Bider the vanity of grieving for those whom we must quickly follow; when I see kings lying by those who deposed them; when I consider rival wits lying side by side; or the holy men that divided the world by their disputes; I reflect with sorrow upon the little competitions, fac- tions, and debates of mankind. When I read the several dates of the 'tombs, of some that died yesterday, and some. six hundred years ago, I consider that great day when we shall all of us be contemporaries, and make our appearance together."

Now whatever sent me to this quotation at such a time? Well, if the cursory reader will turn to it again and reflect upon it a moment, perhaps he will discover that it is not altogether inappropriate.

div.head: In Striking Contrast.
div.p: In Striking Contrast.

At all el-rents, I was pleased by the assurance that the name of the late Alderman Forshaw is to be included among those to be engraved on the inscription. This is an act of justice as well as of grace, such as, if my experience be any criterion, rarely distinguishes municipal corpor- ations. I have in mind the case of a borough in which I resided when its charter was granted. During the period of the first mayoralty the official insignia did not include a chain for the mayoress, and by the time this came to be added, the majority of the members of the town council had taken a dislike to the outgoing mayor—who, sooth to say, was a rather pompous and self- opinionate,d personage, somewhat given to chas- tising with scorpions. As all my readers are aware, it is customary to add to these chains the names of successive‘ holders of office; and, .1- though the lady in question was in all respects worthy, the councillors, while unable to deprive the retiring mayor of his rights in this respect, took adv-antage of a mere accident to exclude the name of his lady, so that the only omission from the mayoress's chain is that of the first and decidedly one of the best of mayoresses. The Warrington Town Council have shown that they are made of better stuff.

div.head: Died For Us.
div.p: Died For Us.

The extensive area served by this paper has already earned considerable distinction for whole-hearted co-operation in all that makes for efficiency in the prosecution of the great war against the Diabolonians whose fiendish barbar- ity has not been paralleled since their worthy allies the Turks, by their inhuman Bashi- Bazouks, earned undying infamy in Bulgaria. The inhabitants of these parts have, according to their several ability, done nobly in further- ance of the cause unselfishly espoused by this 'country in the interests of grievously-wronged and long-suffering Belgium. Better than all else, this district is right worthily represented in the Army and Navy, and has materially helped to ensure a constant succession of sturdy and capable and determined young Men to fill the vacancies caused by casual- ties in the firing line. Happily thus far our men on active service have seemed almost to possess charmed lives; considering the numbers engaged they have been. very fortunate in their com- parative immunity from serious injury. As for those who have unfortunately lost their lives in this unprecedented cataclysm, we shall grate- fully cherish their memories as of neighbours who, in a very real sense, died for us. That they sacrificed themselves absolutely in defence of righteousness were easily demonstrable, but I will not insult the reader's intelligence by again traversing such a well-trodden and familiar path. One has only to think for a single moment what it was that these brave friends of ours went from us to contend against in our behalf and what so many of their surviving comrades continue to fight for on land and sea. Even the more thoughtless may thus realise something of the debt of everlasting obligation which the deaths of our brothers have placed on the community, and these events should in- spire us all to renewed and increased efforts for the ultimate and speedy triumph of our arms in this Titanic struggle between good and evil.
