div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1914.
LYMM.
Citizen Sunday.—November 22 will be observed as Citizen Sunday, when it is expected that the Rev. R. A. Bell, rector of St. Ignatius, Salford, will be the special preacher at the Parish Church.

Wounded Soldiers Expected.—The Red Cross Hospital which has been equipped in Lymm is now ready for the reception of wounded soldiers. It is expected that the first batch will arrive during the week-end. Traders and the Red Cross Society.—The mem- bers of the Lymm Tradesmen's Association at their meeting on Wednesday evening voted three guineas to the Red Cross Society's funds.
Tradesmen's Dinner Abandoned.—The Lymm Tradesmen's Association, at a meeting on Wednesday, decided that, under the present cir- cumstances, they will not hold their annual dinner this year.

Schoolboy Footballers.—Warrington Second- ary School 11. paid a visit to Lynam on Wed- nesday afternoon and easily, beat the local Grammar School's second string by 10 goals to 2. The visitors' scorers were: George (4), Farnell, Dolan and Knowles (2 each). Wednesday Football Team.—The Lymm Wed- nesday Football team journeyed to Gorton this week and made a draw with the Manchester Taxi Drivers. All the scoring was in the first half, Guest securing Lymm's two goals. The visitors were the better team and ought to have won. Next Wednesday the Lymm eleven will entertain the Manchester P.O.

div.head: ABSCONDING REFUGEES. Two Belgians Disappear from Ly-mm.
div.p: ABSCONDING REFUGEES. Two Belgians Disappear from Ly-mm.

Speculation has been rife in Lymm during the week with regard to the whereabouts of two men who arrived at Beechwood last week amongst a party of Belgian refugees. From inquiries made by "The Examiner" reporter in influential quarters, it appears that the conduct of the two men in question was such that it was necessary to speak to them. On Monday they left without giving the offi- cials. any clue as to their destination. In- quiries were made, and it was ascertained that one of the men had given to a Lymm official a different description of his occupation to the one he gave to the London officials, and this fact has given rise to suspicion. It has since been learned that one of the men stated that he had received a fetter from a friend, and that he had made up his mind to go to Ghent, which is at present under German military rule. Another statement is to the effect that the men, afraid of being called upon to join a conscript army, are endeavouring to reach Hol- land so that it will be impossible for the Bel- gian Government to call upon them for service. Mr. Cook, Sir Win. Lever's agent, informed our representative that one of the refugees has received word that the men are in London. However, up to the time of writing the officials at Lymm have received no word from the men.

div.head: RED CROSS WORK. Ways and Means of Equipping Hospital for Wounded DISCUSSED AT PUBLIC MEETING.
div.p: RED CROSS WORK. Ways and Means of Equipping Hospital for Wounded DISCUSSED AT PUBLIC MEETING.

There was a very large attendance at the Lymm Conservative Club on Sunday afternoon, when Mrs. A. Watkin presided over a meeting called to discuss means of equipping and sup- porting a British Red Cross hospital in the village. MANY OFFERS OF HELP.

Mrs. Watkin said that the hospital would have to be a British Red Cross one, and not a general hospital. The Red Cross was the only kind of hospital recognised by the War Office; it was a military affair, and so was under mili- tary supervision. They had a branch of the society in Warrington. It was started when war was declared, as it was thought that the women ought to do their share in helping the country. She (the speaker) and two or three friends met to discuss the matter, and within 24 hours everything had been arranged. Classes for nurses and cooks were initiated, and all the ladits who had volunteered for service were successful in passing the examinations, which were held a few weeks after the courses of instruction had commenced._ _

In the meantime the speaker had had corre- spondence with Mr. John Grundy, who had kindly put his house, Brookfield, at the dis- posal of the committee. This house was ex- ceedingly well adapted for their purposes. The drains had been found satisfactory, and pain- ters and paperhangers were at work—volun- tarily. (Applause.) Many offers of help had been received, but many more were needed. The ladies had done this in small way, and now the moment had arrived when they asked for outside support, and that was the reason for calling the meeting. The women had done a good work and now they came forward to ask the men what they proposed to do. She suggested that they should have a Working Men's Committee, and, if the men could arrange that amongst themselves, one or two could be co-opted on to the Finance Committee. (Applause.) She did not think they could have a better day for the purposes of a meeting of that kind, as it was All Saints' Day. They were all signed with the sign of the Cross, and they should take the Cross up and bear it, re- membering the words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these, my brethren, ye have done it unto Me." (Applause.)

div.head: COMPLEX TASK.
div.p: A COMPLEX TASK.

Mr. W. Pete; Itwywia"n.d—s—sa..id;;;;;." a very great source of satisfaction to all the mere men in Lymm and the surrounding district to see that the ladies had come forward in such a splendid manner in that work. He did not think there were very many districts where the ladies had done so much. Their work was appreciated. (Applause.) It had involved many hours of study and lecturing, and hours of practical work at the Union Workhouse at Warrington. The fact that all the ladies had satisfied the examiners spoke volumes for the earnest way in which they had taken up their duties. (Hear, hear.) There were two organised efforts in con- nection with the war. One was the transport of men and material and the other was the work of tending the wounded. The latter, like the former, was an extremely complex task. The wounded men had to be taken from the trenches and treated at the field hospitals, then passed on to the base hospitals, and then trans- ferred to large Red Cross institutions at home, from whence, in turn, they were dispatched to smaller hospitals, such as the one proposed to be established in the village. The whole of that vast organisation was under the control of the War Office. The hospital which they in- tended to initiate in Lynam would be as much under War Office control as any other sphere of the military operations. It was expected that about 15 wounded soldiers would be received ift Lymm before the end of the present week. Every little district in the country was preparing to do its share of the work. Although the War Office did make a grant, they expected—and quite rightly, too— that the inhabitants in the various districts would lend their support and bear a very sub- stantial share of the cost. The nurses had given their services, Mr. Grundy had provided the house, and various others had lent help. How- ever, there would have to be three trained nurses.

To Cost About £lO per Week. The hospital would involve expense, and, ir it was to be run efficiently and satisfactorily, a weekly outlay of about £lO would be necessary. When they realised what the soldiers had done he did not think they would grndge any ex- pense they might be put to, or any assistance they might offer. He had no doubt that Mrs. Watkin would get the necessary amount as easily as drinking tea. (Laughter.) The move- ment was one for all classes, and it would be a pleasing thing if the whole of the district could be worked by a Working Men's Com- mittee. Miss Sylvia Broadbent gave details of experi- ence gained in fitting up the Raddon. Court Hospital, Latchford, and the cost thereof, add- ing that all the trouble and expense was worth while when they saw the gallant men comfort- ably settled down and gradually getting stronger day by day. (Applause.) Mr. J. Holt stated that the Congregational Sunday School had given the money—amount- ing to XS—which they had set aside for their annual trip, to the Lymm Branch of the Bri-
tish Red Cross Society. (Applause.) Mrs. Watkin said that that was the kind of feeling that was wanted.
PRESENT COMMITTEE.

In reply to a question it was stated that the present committee consisted of Mrs. Watkin, district leader; Miss Groves, commandant; Miss Boumphrey, quartermaster; Dr. Thorpe, admin- istrator of the hospital; with Doctors Burrows, De Jong and H. Thorpe as assistants; Mr. Giles Hunt, honorary secretary and treasurer; with the following general members: Mesdames Moseley, Beckett, Groves, Arthur Bleckly and Hartley, and Miss Garton; Messrs. A. B. Boumphrey, W. N. Molesworth, A. de Clifford Parmit,er, J. Garton and F. E. Evans.

div.head: MEN'S SHARE.
div.p: THE MEN'S SHARE.

At the conclusion of the meeting it was decided that the men shall have a meeting amongst themselves to decide upon what course they will take i the matter. It was eventually decided that a committee of men should be formed, and at a meeting on Wednesday the necessary officials were elected.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH

Four New Street Lamps.--At a meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday, the Deputy-Clerk reported that four lamps were being fixed in Red-lane, and that the sub-com- mittee had indicated to the foreman from the Warrington Corporation Gas Department where the lamps had to be fixed. The rate would be the same as for other lamps in the parish. St. Thomas' Band of Hope.—A large number of the members of this Band of Hope spent a merry evening together on Thursday, when a number of amusing competitions were indulged in. As the members left for home they were presented with parcels of toffee, which had been given by Mesdames Milling, Stannard, Whiteman, Hallows, Newhall, Knight, the Misses Edgerley and Willett, the Vicar (the Rev. J. Collins) and Mr. Mynekyme.

div.head: GRAPPENHAL L.
div.p: GRAPPENHAL L.

A Drainage Question.—lt was reported at the Runcorn Rural District Council meeting on Tuesday that the Grappenhall Local Sewerage Committee had inspected the ditch below May- field-road and had resolved that the Public Health Surveyor be asked to prepare and sub- mit a plan and estimate for the work of dealing with the sewage from the vicinity of Mayfield- road.—On the proposition of Councillor Pilling, seconded by Councillor Lister-Kaye, the report was adopted.

div.head: GREAT SANK EY.
div.p: GREAT SANK EY.

C.E.M.S.—The quarterly meeting of the San- key Church of England Men's Society was held on Sunday afternoon, when Mr. Laws, the Warrington Police Court Missioner, gave an address. Everywhere, he said, they could see placards saying "Your King and country need you," and, just as the country was calling for men, so was the Church, who was waging war against sin. To Learn the Reason Why !—No satisfactory report having been received with reference to compensation for the roads at Burtonwood having been damaged owing to the diversion of traffic on account of the new Sankey Canal Bridge, the Rural District Council decided on Wednesday that the Chairman kMr. -W. Fur- ness) and representatives of the townships affected should meet the County Roads Com- mittee on the matter.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

"Six Hundred Miles up the Nile."—Mr. G. E. Thompson, of Liverpool, gave the second half of his interesting lecture, "Six Hundred Miles up the Nile," at the Friends' School on Monday evening, his remarks being illustrated by a number of beautiful lantern slides, made from photographs taken by himself. Wesley Guild Discuss the War.—At a meeting of the Wesley Guild on Wednesday evening, Mr. C. E. Parker gave an address on "Christianity and the War." In the course of his remarks he insisted that the Church should recognise the right of ally country to fight against a signatory Power who broke its word to a weaker Power. After the address a number of the members •joined in a discussion on the subject. Youthful Horticultucists.—On Friday after- noon last the prizes gained by the successful scholars in the competitions organised in con- nection with the Penketh and Sankey Flower Show were distributed by Mrs. J. G. Within- shaw. Dr. Murray presided over the brief pre- sentation ceremony, which took place in the Council School. The prize list was as follows: Wild flower bouquet (presented by the society) : 1, E. Backhouse; 2, J. S. Thomas; 3, A. Ains- worth. Tray of wild flowers (prizes given by Mr. Withinshaw) : 1, D. Bingham, Sankey School; 2, N. Backhouse. Tray of wild ,flow- ers (given by Mr. Withinshaw) : 1, D. Bing- ham; 2, N. Leigh; 3, E. Goulden. Essay on wild flowers (given by Mr. Aldcroft): 1, Lily Bailey; 2, W. Pye; 3, W. Hunter. Coloured illustrations of plants (given by Mrs. Dodds, Mr. Backhouse and Dr. Murray) : 1, Hilda Ray; 2, E. Hatton; 3, Annie Dunabin. Council School gardens (given by the society): 1, B. Loaley and R. Fisher; 2. J. Kilehaw and A. Owen; 3, N. Leigh and J. Atherton. Special prizes (given by Mr. Griffiths): J. Kilshaw and I. Maines.

div.head: REFUGEES AS HOSTS.
div.p: REFUGEES AS HOSTS.
Afternoon Tea at Hall Nook.

, On Wednesday afternoon the Belgian refugees held the first of a series of afternoon teas at Hall Nook, Penketh. Admission was by tickets, which cost 6d. each. Their corfimittee have ar- ranged these teas as a pleasant way of keeping in touch with those who wish them well and also to help to form a fund for the special benefit of the women, when the time comes for their re- turn to their own homeland. A very pleasant afternoon was spent in the grounds, and with music and singing. Some of the Belgian girls, who were prettily dressed in the national colours, sang songs in their own tongue, and, of course, gave the visitors the Belgian National Anthem.. They were accompanied on the piano by a Belgian lady.

div.head: ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE HELP.
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE HELP.

On behalf of the Belgian Refugee Committee, Dr. Murray wrote to the Warrington Assess- ment Committee asking for a reduction in the assessment of Hall Nook, pointing out that it was let at a nominal rent of £1 per annum. The old assessment was £94, and the com- mittee yesterday decided to make a reduction to a nominal assessment of £1 per annum. HELP OUT OF PLEASURE. In aid of the fund for the Belgian refugees a whist drive and dance was held in the Great Sankey Sunday school on Friday evening of last week, when about 180 parishioners and friends assembled and spent a pleasant evening together. The prize-winners in the drive were: Mesdames Denny and Parsonage and Miss Ulverston, and Messrs. Phelps, E. Darlington and B. Ireland. After cards came dancing, which was kept up merrily to music supplied by Messrs. Hall Bros., of Penketh. Messrs. E. J. Dumbill and H. Davies had charge of the drive and Messrs. W. Dwerryhouse and B. Ray were the M.C.'s for the dancing. During the evening the Vicar (the Rev. J. R. Jones) said the Belgians had gone through a great ,deal of suffering and were de- serving of all the aid that this country could give them. The world had never before seen such a terrible war, and he hoped that those who could not go into the firing line would endeavour to do useful work at home.

div.head: REFUGEES' CLEAN HEALTN BILL,
div.p: REFUGEES' CLEAN HEALTN BILL,

At a meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council on Wednesday, Dr. Sephton Medi- cal Officer) reported that he had visited Hall Nook, Penketh, and had found the Belgian families comfortable and free from disease. They had all been vaccinated, except one of the children, which Dr. Murray had promised to vaccinate very soon.

div.head: PAD GATE.
div.p: PAD GATE.

Wesley Guild.—The devotional meeting of the Wesley Guild was held on Monday evening, and was presided over by Mr. F. Wright. Short papers were read by Messrs. H. Monks and W. Seed, whose subjects were "The Labourers in the Vineyard" and "Silent Preachers" respec- tively. The roV of honour of those who have joined the Army from the Padgate Guild was read, and Dr. Bennett paid a warm tribute to each of the members named, saying how proud he was of them and expressing the hope that all would come back safe and sound. Mr. H. Tomlin presented to the Guild a beautiful hand-painted card, upon which the names are to be inscribed and kept in remembrance of those who have so nobly offered their services to the country. During the evening Miss Duckworth sang a solo entitled "A hymn for the present time."

div.head: "DISGRACE TO CIVILISED PEOPLE." Residents' Forceful Description of Defective Drainage.
div.p: "DISGRACE TO CIVILISED PEOPLE." Residents' Forceful Description of Defective Drainage.
Padgate sewerage arrangements constituted the chief topic discussed at the monthly meet- ing of the Warrington District Council, held in Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday, Councillor Furness. presiding.

The Clerk read -a letter from Mr. W. Bennett, Bruche Farm, in which he stated: "I have written the President of the Local Government Board about the disgraceful state of the drain- age round Bruche. I wrote to Councillor Maher and the Surveyor some time since, and they treated the matter very lightly in my opinion. I don't wish to die of typhoid before my time, nor for my family to die. We have one boy on the farm with a bad throat, and I lost a cow with violent dysentery two weeks ago, I presume through drinking the water. The stench in the dry weather is something vile. I don't want to go behind your backs in ,the mat- ter, but certainly the sanitation in this locality is a disgrace to civilisation. Fifty pounds spent in pipes would obviate the nuisance, and if the Council will not take the matter up I must work on my own."_

The Clerk: I acknowledged that letter. The Chairman said that the,District Council had been prepared for a long time to carry out a scheme, but the Parish Council had not seen their way to accept it. The fault was not entirely that of the District Council, but that of the Parish Council, in their not beipg pre- pared to accept the schemes which the District Council had suggested.

div.head: Complaint to the Local Government Board.
div.p: Complaint to the Local Government Board.

The Clerk then read a letter which the Local Government Board had sent, enclosing the letter which Mr. Bennett had forwarded to them "with reference to the alleged nuisance from a ditch in your neighbourhood." The letter re- quested that the Board might be furnished with the observations of the Council on the com- munication.

Mr. Bennett's letter to the Local Government Board was as follows :—" I ask your considera- tion regarding the sewerage in this village (Padgate). There is a ditch, or, rather, an open sewer, running close to my house which is a disgrace to any civilised people. This summer it has been worse than ever. I cannot get the District Council to move in the matter at all. This ditch could be piped for 150 or 200 yards to obviate the nuisance very consider- ably at a small cost lt is really a source of danger to health and I dread a visi- tation of typhoid. To-night my wife and my- self were really upset after passing this ditch, and, if possible, I should like you to send some independent person to have a look at it. I don't think you will find anything like it anywhere in the country. It is caused by the drainage of Fearnhead and Padgate, I believe, all coming down this ditch. There being no sewerage scheme there is no fall, and the sew- age collects more like a cesspool than any other thing. I am one of the largest ratepayers, farm- ing 350 acres. I don't see why we should be poisoned through other people's property. I dare not let any of my cattle drink the water, because if I did it would cause a lot of sickness in the district.' The Council fenced most of the brook about two years ago. "A month since I lost a healthy cow from dysentery. I cannot prove she drank the water, but I put her death down to this. Trusting you will give the matter your attention at your earliest convenience." A Growing District.
. The Surveyor explained that only the sewer- age of Padgate went down the ditch, and not that of Fearnhead.

The Chairman said that if anything had been submitted to the Parish Council they had re- fused to accept it. It had always been the principle with the District Council to try to work in harmony with the Parish Council, and they did not want to thrust a gigantic or over- bearing sewerage scheme on the parish. That justified the District Council in asking the Parish Council to accept the suggested schemes. There was a minimised scheme, which would cost about £75, And which would meet the objections and conditions which Mr. Bennett raised in his letter. They were prepared to send that scheme to the Chairman of the Parish. Council for their consideration. If they did not consider it favourably he thought the Dis- trict Council would be justified in accepting the-scheme and putting the cost on the parish. Councillor Dennett said that as he had lived in Padgate for ten years he knew the conditions and the cause of the trouble. Several houses had been built since he went to the village, some of them with water closets upstairs. There was no satisfactory sewerage arrange- ments, and as the houses were mostly Mr. Bennett's property, he was the cause of the nuisance himself.
The Chairman: He contributes. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: His statement to the Local Government Board is a very partial one.

The Chairman: It is not quite the truth. An Unfulfilled Promise. Rev. A. M. Mitchell: I think the Local Gov- ernment Board ought to have the whole state- ment, because he is giving a wrong impression. Councillor Dennett spoke of difficulties which he had experienced in the district, and after further discussion, The Clerk said that the District Council had promised the Local Government Board to do something in the matter, and they had not carried out their promise. Dr. Sephton (Medical Officer) : You will al- ways have trouble so long as you patch up. You must go in for a thorough scheme for Padgate and Fearnhead. If you don't, you will still have the trouble. I have written to the Local Government Board repeatedly, saying that a scheme was in hand, but the matter remains where it was ten years ago. Something ought to be done on an extensive scale which would be permanent and a comfort to the whole dis- trict, as well as a credit to the district.
The Surveyor said that the £75 mentioned would not cover more than the cost of piping. He suggested that the cost would be about £lBO. The Clerk: Did the Parish Council assent to this?

The Surveyor: The matter stands at present. I gave Mr. Mather a copy of the two estimates and he said: "Keep them back and I will put them before the Parish Council." Not the Time for a Bip Scheme. The Clerk: The Parish Council said that what was now being suggested would be suffi- cient for the purpose and they have not asked you to carry it out. Councillor Dennett thought the time was in- opportune for a large scheme, owing to so many calls being made on account of the war. A scheme to last four or five years would do until things got settled down. The Chairman asked what the ..ClBO scheme suggested by the Surveyor would do. The Surveyor: Carry the whole of the ,Pad- gate sewerage to a point further on. The Clerk read a letter which he had sent the Local Government Board on the 4th April, 1013, in which he stated that the Parish Coun- cil had protested against a scheme, and in view of that the District Council was of the opinion that the scheme should be left in abeyance for the present, and _that the Surveyor should be instructed to make arrangements for the peri- odical cleaning out of the foul ditches. The Clerk added that he did not want to write in a similar strain now, but wanted to know* what the Council were prepared to do. Eventually it was decided to write the Local Government Boaid to the effect that the Coun- cil had given attention to the letters and had instructed the Surveyor to report on the whole matter at the next meeting. Meanwhile Coun- cillor Mather and Mr. Newcombe would report to the Parish Council. Councillor Backhouse: It should be im- pressed on them that we have not lost sight of , this platter. (Hear, ,hear.)

div.head: CHAPLAIN AND FEVER.
div.p: CHAPLAIN AND FEVER.
Rev. H. F. S. Collier's Reasons for Discontinuing Visits

div.head: TO COTTAGE HOMES.
div.p: TO COTTAGE HOMES.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, Mr. A. J. Jolley presiding, a letter was read from the Rev. H. F. S. Collier, chaplain at the Cottage Homes, informing the Board that he had re- ceived orders from the War Office to the effect that he had been appointed one of.f our chaplains in the West Lancashire- Division as from October 16th. He had arranged with the Rev. H. I. Wadeson, rector of Croft, to see the children at the -homes until a curate-in-charge had been appointed. The curate would then attend to all duties connected with the office during his (Mr. Collier's) absence.

div.head: WHY HE STAYED AWAY!
div.p: WHY HE STAYED AWAY!
Referring to the ,serious outbreak of scarlet fever in the homes, Mr. Collier wrote:—

_ "Up to the time that this broke out I was visiting the homes weekly and taking two classes per week. When the disease spread I considered it advisable to discontinue my visits for the following reasons: (1) I had four little children of, my own all under eight. It was not fair ndr right to run any risk of bringing back scar- let fever into my home. I am not a doctor. (2) Constantly mixing, as I did, with the 300 children in our schools, if was not fair nor right to run any risk of spreading the disease in our own schools. (3) I have made 240 visits in the village in ten weeks, and some of these were sick visits. It is not fair to. the sick, to maternity cases, &T., to first visit a place that must be full of scarlet fever germs. The chil- dren at the Cottage Homes have not been to church for the same reason, but have been prac- tically isolated from the children in the village. I have never been expected to visit where there are zymotic diseases, either as curate, vicar, or chaplain, and hence I hope that you will realise that it was not for myself, but for the sake of my own children, other people's children, and my own sick folk that I had to discontinue for a while my work amongst the' kiddies 'at the homes, which work is very dear to my heart."

div.head: CHAPLAIN'S SURPRISE.
div.p: THE CHAPLAIN'S SURPRISE.

The Clerk: On receipt of this letter I sent the resolution passed at the last meeting to Mr. Collier, who replied: "I can only say that I am very surprised and very hurt at the reso- lution which was adopted by the Guardians at their last meeting. My answer is in my letter, •which I wrote you yesterday."

o The resolution referred 0 by the Clerk was contained in the minutes of the Padgate Romes Committee, which were adopted. It read as follows: "It was moved by Mr. Brooks, and seconded by Mr.. Ritchie, that the salary of the chaplain be reduced by per annum as a protest against his failure to efficiently perform his duties at the homes since the outbreak of scarlet fever.—An amendment was moved by the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, seconded by Mr. McKinley, that the Clerk be instructed to write the chap- lain expressing the surprise of the Guardians at his neglect of his duties since the outbreak of scarlet fever at the homes, and to express the hope that no further cause for complaint would arise.—The amendment was carried." .

div.head: NOT "PERAMBULATING DISEASE MACHINES." _ _ _
div.p: NOT "PERAMBULATING DISEASE MACHINES." _ _ _
Mr. McKinley :1 don't admire him when he says he was not obliged to attend such cases. I think people need more spiritual attention at a time of sickness. . _ _
The Chairman: At the same time they should not be perambulating disease machines. I think the reverend gentlemam has made a very fair statement. 11 - . - -

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: I understand that the Rev. Mr. Chamberlain, late chaplain of 7ainhill Asylum, has been appointed curate-in- charge at Padgate. He will have no fear of such a small matter as scarlet fever. The Chairman: I don't think it is fair that such a remark should pass without remon- strance. It is not a question of fear at all, but of a man with a duty to his fellow creatures. He has taken wise precautions to avoid the spread of disease. To suggest this action was Prompted by cowardice is very unworthy. Mr. Dennett : I am sure Mr. Collier is by no means a coward, and no more afraid of disease than my reverend friend here. Mr. Brooks thought it was cowardice to neg- lect these children during sickness. Mr. Dennett : How many visits were made by the Roman Catholic chaplain? Mr. McKinley: He went just the same all the time.

The Chairman: I would leave it to the com- mon-sense of the general public. If anyone will peruse the letter without passion or prejudice they will see he has behaved like an honourable, straightforward and wise man in considering the interests of the parish. Mr. McKinley: I take exception to the part of his letter where he says he has not been expected to visit such cases.

div.head: TEMPORARY ARRANGEMENT
div.p: A TEMPORARY ARRANGEMENT

The Chairman: The question is: "Is the Board willing to accept the ministrations of Mr. Wadeson and also the new rate-in-charge, when he takes up his duties?" Mr. Mather: The Rev. Chamberlain has earned his pension at Rainhill. lam sorry Mr. Wadeson is not taking on that duty all the_time. Mr. Collier is away. - Mr. Bent: I should he pleased if Mr. Wadeson would take up the duties regularly. I don't see why Mr._ Collier should appoint a chaplain.

21ie Chairman : It is it-temporary arrange_ meat. ' Mr. Bent: We don't know how long Mr. Col- lier may he away. He may he au-ay for I') months. Mr. Wadeson will cease to attend the schools after Mr. Chamberlain arrives. Mr. Mather: I have nothing against Mr. Chamberlain, but I know Mr. Wadeson. It was decided that the suggestion of the Rev. IT. F. R. Collier be adopted by the Board. Mrs. Collinglyood : Will he attend the schools when there is an epidemic? Mr. Mather: Mr. Wadeson will, and I daresay Mr. Chamberlain will.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
A meeting of this District Council was held on Tuesday at Dutton, Mr. C. E. Linaker, sen., presiding.
A DIFFICULT PROBLEM.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board, in reply to a resolution passed by the local authorities who contribute towards the salary and expenses of the additional inspector for Widnes and the neighbourhood under the Alkali, &c., Works Regulation Act, 1906, im- pressing on the Board the desirability of making an order, under Section 8 of the Act, as regards copper smelting works. The Board referred the Council to a letter addressed to them on Decem- ber 18th last, and stated that nothing had occurred to alter the view expressed in the last paragraph of that letter. In this connection attention was drawn to the following remarks as to smelting works in the annual report (1913) of the Chief Inspector: "Further advance was =Fie during 1913 in the prevention of the escape of metallic fumes from these works, and also in the reduction of the average proportion of acid escaping, with chimney gases, from all the works under inspection. In the case of lead smelting and copper smelting works, how- ever, the reduction in acidity of the escaping chimney gases was still a problem difficult of practical_ _solution."
In our district the damage is very marked.

PROPOSED NEW ROAD. The Chairman referred to the suggested new road from Ellesmere Port in the direction of Helsby, by way of Thornton. The Chester Rural District Council, he said, had appointed a small committee to go over the area, and the Ellesmere Port Urban Authority were anxiously awaiting their report. The road would con- cern the County Council, the Wirral District Council, the Ellesmere Port Urban District Council and the Runcorn Rural District Coun- cil. Although they in the Runcorn Courgicil area would have no jurisdiction over the road, it would open out an important district, in Helsby and Ellesmere Port. He suggested that a committee should be appointed to go into the whole matter. It would cut off gx or seven miles in approaching an important district. A committee was appointed, consisting of the following: The Chairman, and Messrs. Blythe, Basnett, Harrison, Houghton, Woodward and
RUNCORN GUARDIANS. Mr. Spruce presided over the forAtnios meeting of the Runcorn Board of Dutton on Tuesday.

div.head: BAKER'S BRILLIANT RUN.
div.p: BAKER'S BRILLIANT RUN.

Baker was responsible for what was, perhaps, the most brilliant piece of individual work of the afternoon. Taberner, when well within Warrington's preserves, secured the ball and it immediately travelled across to Baker. Then followed a neck-and-neck race to the line be- tween Baker and several of the Salford men, and owing to his fine turn of speed the War- rington lad gained on his adversaries, and, after running over half the length of the field, regis- tered a beautiful try, which, however, went unconverted, Tranter failing with the kick. This effort on Baker's part was greatly to the tazte of the spectators, who evidenced their approval after the customary manner. In the closing stages of the game the Reds struggled hard to reduce the adverse balance, and kept the home team hemmed in their own quarters, but the defence proved superior to the attack, until just on time. Then it was that Bevan managed to snap up the ball and nip over the line, thus securing the easiest try of the whole match. He also took the goal-kick, but his attempt was a failure. When the final whistle sounded the score read: Warrington, 2 goals 6 tries (22 points); Salford, 2 goals 2 tries (10 points). HOW THE PLAYERS PLAYED.

Saturday's waz by no means a ;la-tell-victory for Warrington, but was the reward of superior merit. Both fore and aft—indeed, in every department—they were the better team. Tran- ter played a splendid game all through, and it is not too much to say that he was the most versatile and useful man on the field. He would still have been the pick of the players even had he not performed the "hat trick." Jolley was quite superior to his vis-a-vis. The Warrington threequarters showed more alert- ness than did the Salford quartet. John, the visitors' half-back, and his colleague, Waite, undoubtedly played excellently, but they lacked the initiative and resourcefulness which was displayed by Dainteth and Young. The War- rington forwards were all seen to advantage, and the aid they rendered to their side could not be over-rated.

div.head: MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
RYLANDS' RECS. v. WEASTE.

These teams met at Salford on Saturday in the first division of the above League, there being a fair attendance. Rylands', who were short of Povey, won the toss, and Weaste kicked off. The ball immediately travelled to Warren, who, eluding several opponents, passed to A. Horrocks. The latter gave to Rowlinson, who scored Under the posts in the first minute, War- ren goaling. After this reverse Weaste played up and kept Rylands' busy defending. F. Hor- rocks eventually found touch well inside the home half, and from the scrummage Warren swung the ball out to Potter, who dropped a grand goal. Ryland? again got their passing machinery at work, and Warren, beating several of the Weaste men, gave the ball to Smith, who scored under the posts, Warren again. goaling. Just before the interval Griffiths, after running half the length of the field, scored a good try, Potter failing at goal. Half-time arrived with the score: Rylands', 3 goals 3 tries (15 points); Weaste, nil. _

„ The second half commenced in rare style. Clifford went from half-back to full-hack, and played a grand game in the new position. Fin- nigan took his old place, the change making a great improvement in the Weaste team. Both ends were visited in turn, Rylands' failing to break through the defence until about half-way through the moiety, when F. Horrocks, fielding the ball, and beating man after man, gave a lightning pass to Warren, who, taking the ball at top speed, scored under the posts. The same player goaled. Afterwards Weaste enjoyed a spell of attacking, and Finnigan made a grand run on his wing, but failed at the final pass. When time was called the score read: Rylands', 4 goals 4 tries (20 points); Weaste, nil. The outstanding players .werei F. Horrocks, Warren, Potter and A. Stretford for Rylands', and R. Clifford and Finnigan for Weaste.

div.head: NO MATCH. Wigan and Reduced War-Time Wages.
div.p: NO MATCH. Wigan and Reduced War-Time Wages.
PLAYERS' STRIKE. Warriagtoes Position Fang Explained.

There will be no Northern Union match against Wigan to-day, either at Warrington or Wigan: Mr. T. P. Bradshaw, honorary secretary of the Warrington Club, wishes us. to make it clear that his committee have opposed, still oppose, and will continue to oppose, the policy of the majority of the N.U. League clubs which lays it down that the wages of the players shall be reduced by 25 per cent. At the beginning of the season his committee and the players mutually arranged that if the war adversely affected revenue, they would agree to a revision of the rate of vk ages, and it is thought that that friendly arrangement ought to have been allowed to otand. Both players and committee still favour that method of dealing with any financial trouble which may arise. _ _

The matches for to-day have been cancelled owing to the Wigan players refusing to accept the 25 per cent, reduction of wages decided on by the Northern League meeting. Representatives of the Wigan Club waited on the meeting in Manchester on Tuesday and stated that their players refused to accept the reduction of wages as required by the resolu- tion adopted at the recent special general meet- ing of League clubs, and asked the League Management Committee to waive the rule for the time being and await developments. The Management Committee pointed out: (1) That they have no power to waive or amend the resolution adopted; (2) that the agreement be- tween clubs and players is a payment per match only and clubs are committing no breach of such agreement if they do not sialect any player to play in matches until he agrees to accept the reduction required; (3) that the position is considered of such a serious nature that it is thought better that unwilling players should be sacrificed rather than the existence of the clulfs membership; (4) that any breach of resolution by any club will be looked upon as a serious matter, and will be dealt with as such.

div.head: MINDS FULLY MADE U.
div.p: MINDS FULLY MADE U.

The Wigan players met the committee on Thursday night to discuss the situation. At the close Mr. J. Counsell (Chairman of the club) announced the unanimous resolve of the players, and said there was no alternative but to cancel the matches of both first and second teams with Warrington. They had thought there was a possible chance of the --players coming to another decision on the matter, but it was evident that they had already fully made up their minds on the subject.
-Yesterday Mr. Bradshaw received an official communication from the Wigan Club to the effect that to-day's matches would be cancelled. WARRINGTON_ REM:Iy TO "CARRY ON."

_ . . We understand that the Warrington players have not said anything officially about the re- duction, notice of which had been posted in the club rooms. The decision of the Wigan players has caused quite a stir in football circles. At a meeting of the Warrington Committee on Wednesday evening the following were selected to play against Wigan, in the event of the match coming off :---Jolley; Taberner, Brad- shaw, Tranter and Baker; Dainteth and Young; Cox, Clare, Cunliffe, Green, Mather and Critch- ley. It will be noticed that Fearnley was not included in the team selected, not having recovered from injuries received the previous Saturday.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
MATCHES FOR TO-DAY.
Bank Quay Recs. v. Newton Cons; referee, Mr. G. Knight.
Hollis Green v. Elmwoca Cons; Mr. J. T. Hadkiss.
Orford White Star v. St. Barnabas% Mr. W. Bennett.
Earlestown Y.M.C.A. V. Fairfield united; Mr. J. Smith.
Earlestown St. John's Mission v. Paddington; Mr. B. Howell.
Warrington Central V. Longford United; Mr. H. G. Brandreth.
NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Stockton Heath V. Cadishead Wesleyans. ITEMS.
Latchford Baptists have found the turn in the long lane.
They scored their first point of the season on Saturday, sharing half and half with Fairfield Athletic.

- Wyatt has proved a capture for the BaptitSis. Monks and Johnson were the Athletic's strong est players. Monks, who is in the Territorial forces, and, consequently, a "Terrier," proved a terror as well.
There will be rejoicing in the Baptists' camp now.

Paddington's ground and accommodation is second to none of all the teams in the League. Craik was a notable absentee last week. Wrench was overshadowed by Denny at centre-half. Gregory and Pilling were a better pair of defenders than Holmes and Spencer. George proved himself a capable custodian. Miller had not many opportunities of showing his ability. Holcroft is a very speedy winger.
Maddock was below his usual form.
T. Smith (a late Heathen) was absent oling to illness.

There is plenty of interest in the Paddington Club. Marsh is able to get about again after his recent accident. Newton Cons, were defeated 3-0 by their near rivals, but the score did not represent the run of the play. The Mission lads mace profit of their opportu- nities, whilst the Cons. hesitated and lost their chances.
Dagnall was very good in goal and Tithers was a good defender. • Smart disappointed his colleagues when he missed that penalty.
- Massey, Winders and Griffiths performed well for the Mission.
---- - There was a keen struggle between the United and the Y.M.C:A. ,

Millward and Goulden were keen opponents. Martin and Potter proved very safe in their respective goals. Ditchfield was the best of the home half-back line, but Bebbington and Payne ran him very close. The FM. forwards showed better combination than did the United front line. Millward's goal was a splendid individual effort. Elmwood continue to disappoint their sup- porters. Lamb was their outstanding player, against Longford. Fairfield United retain their position at the head of the chart, and Latchford Baptists are still holders of "the wooden spoon." Padgate vanquished Daresbury in a "friendly" on Saturday. In the first half they had a clear lead of three goals, but they only managed to finish up one to the good. ' Higginson showed that he knows the way to the goal. S. Hardman failed to score against Daresbury. Did he leave his shooting boots at home? Gilbert is now playing on the top of his form for Padgate. It was hard lines that Padgate's latest capture should get injured in his first match with his new club. Sankey Athletic suffered in their game with Beamont United on Saturday from the fact that they were without their regular goalkeeper— , Gleave. His place was taken by Beddard.
Baptists Gain Their First League Point,

div.head: LONGFORD UNITED'S DECISIVE WIN.
div.p: LONGFORD UNITED'S DECISIVE WIN.

Saturday's Warrington and District League fixtures produced a crop of very interesting encounters. So far this season there is a marked advance on the quality of play as compared with last year. It is not so much a question of the superiority of any one team above the others, but a general levelling up, with the result that there are keener games, and in consequence greater interest is evident amongst the players. The Orford White Star, who have done well lately visited Paddington, and were again_ suc- cessful in annexing both points. The first half was scoreless, George, in the home goal, being chiefly responsible for this. In the second half the Star forwards shone more brightly, and scored twice, the home team being unable to respond. Latchford Baptists of late have been showing improved form, and on Saturday they notched ' their first League point of the season. In Wyatt they have secured a capable goalkeeper, but the backs in front of him are not very safe. During the past month Fairfield Athletic have not made the progress that was expected of them, having only gained a point out of their last four matches. _ _ _

The game between Fairfield United and the Y.M.C.A., as the score of one goal each indi- cates, was a fast and keenly-fought contest, And in the return match to-day there should be a big 'crowd to witness the game. St. Barnabas' easily accounted for Hollins Green in their return fixture by putting up four goals to nil. Elmwood Congregationalists still continue on the losing side, and on Saturday they were again defeated on their own ground, this time by Longford United, the score being 5-0.
Notes by "Linesman."

an equalising point, being at length rewarded. Pearson fed his wings well and led many a raid on the visitors' goal, and it was from one of them Clarke put the teams on even terms. Re- sult : Latchford Baptists, 3 goals; Fairfield Ath- letic, 3 goals.

PADDINGTON V. ORFORD WHITE STAR. Much interest was displayed in the meeting of the above clubs,. as the visitors had been creat- ing a great reputation for themselves by their performances during the last few weeks, and the home team had made up their minds to do their best to check their opponents' victorious career. Neither team was at full strength, Craik stand- ing down from the home eleven in consequence of an old injury asserting itself, whilst T. Smith did not figure in the visitors' ranks owing to illness. The following players turned out before a fair number of spectators:— _ .

Paddington: George; Holmes and Spencer; Smith, Wrench and Garnett; Holcroft, Bleas- dale, Woodhead, Darbyshire and Hepperd. White Star: Miller; Pilling and Gregory; Gifford, Denny and Caldwell; Maddock, Meachin, Hankinson, Stubbs and Dunbobbin. The referee was Mr. J. Smith. The home team won the choice of ends and played against the breeze. The opening stages were of a very keen and fast charaeter, but, owing to fine kicking by the respective backs, play was chiefly in midfield. After ten min- utes had elapsed the visitors, asserting their superiority, made several dangerous raids on the home citadel, and it was only the zpod work of the backs and of George in goal that pre- vented a score being made. The home team occasionally broke away, but the visitors' half- back line proved to be a strong barrier against • them, and time and again broke up their efforts. Woodhead; on one occasion, made a good indi- vidual effort, but his shot hit the foot of the post and bounced out of play. After this the visitors attacked very strongly, and gained several corner kicks, but they failed to improve upon them, George, on several occasions, clear- ing when his backs were beaten. After a spell of mid-field play, the home forwards improved, and Holcroft led several attacks on the visitors' goal, but Gregory and Pilling proved very safe. As the interval was drawing near the visitors gained a corner kick. This was well placed by Maddock, and just as the whistle' blew to cease operations the ball was put between the posts. The point did not count. At half-time there was no score.

On resuming, the visitors re-arranged their forward line, Hankinson going to outside left. The visitors at once set up a fast pace and played a keener game than in the first half. The home backs stuck to their positions, and were successful in repelling several dangerous attacks, but at length Meachin got through and scored the opening goal of the match. The home team made a determined effort to get on level terms. Holcroft continually beat his opponent, and, being well served by his turn of speed, led several attacks on the visitors' goal, but Gregory and Pilling always cleared their lines without Miller being troubled. The visitors increased their lead from a penalty kick given against one of the home backs, and the home goal was again in danger from another free kick just outside the penalty area. The homesters attacked strongly and would have scored but for the timely intervention of Denny. At the call of time play was being contested in the home half. Result: Orford White Star, 2 goals; Padding- ton, nil. FAIRFIELD UNITED v. EARLESTOWN Y.M.C.A.
These, teams met for the first time on Satur- day at Orford-road. Great interest was shown in the match, and there was a good number of supporters present when the following players turned out:—
Fairfield United: Potter; Kelly and Wood- house; Ditchfield, Bebbington and Payne; Roberts, Scott, Millward, Poulter and S. Wood- house.

Y.M.C.A. : Martin; Birkett and Page; Fair- hurst, Goulden and Atkinson; Taylor, Hughes, Riley, Oilman and Lee. *A The referee was Mr. G. Bamber. The home team had choice of ends, and Riley set the ball in motion. The visitors soon raided the home quarters, but Payne relieved with a huge kick. The visitors were showing to the best advantage, and were soon attacking again. Following up a mistake by Woodhouse, Taylor got through and beat Potter with a hard drive ten minutes from the start. This reverse roused the homesters, and they made a determined struggle to get on level terms. Millward, beat- ing two opponents, shot hard for goal, Martin only making a partial clearance. If inward fol- lowed up, and putting the ball between the posts made the scores equal. The spectators warmly applauded the effort. Both teams now strove hard for a lead, but in spite of the deter- mined efforts of the forwards, the defenders per- formed better still, and held them at bay. At the interval the score was one goal each. . .

The second half opened at a fast pace, and the bal travelled quickly from end to end, but again the defenders proved themselves better 1 than the attackers. At the end of a keen and well-fought game the result was a draw of one goal each. ELMWOOD CONS. V. LONGFORD UNITED. These teams met on the ground of the former in Manchester-road. The Cons., won the toss and started with the wind at their backs. Brown set the ball rolling and at once made tracks for the home goal, where Jas. Mellor re- lieved. Even play followed for a short time, and then the visitors assumed the upper hand and attacked the home citadel, Norke, the cus- todian, being penalised for carrying the ball. Stevens took the kick. The homesters packed their goal and the ball was got away. Not to be denied, the visitors returned to the attack, and Phcenix conceded a corner. The flag kick being well placed in front of goal, Finch opened the score for the visitors. From the centre kick the homesters failed to break down the visitors' de- fence, and were quickly driven on to the defen- sive again. Norke was a second time penalised for holding. Stevens again took the kick and scored the visitors' second goal. At the interval the visitors were leading by 2 goals to nil. . . .

On resuming the visitors led off with an 'attack, but Jas. Mellor cleared just in the nick of time. Smart gained possession and beating a couple of opponents, passed out to Sherratt, who promptly drove the •leather past Norke and scored a third goal for the United. Encouraged by these successes the United players monopo- lised the game for a time. Good play by Finch re- pulsed• an attack, but shortly afterwards Hands added a fourth goal, subsequently scoring again from a free kick awarded against Mellor. From thence on until the finish the homesters showed better form, hut the inside forwards failed to utilise openings made by Lamb on the extreme left. The visitors' backs had not much difficulty in clearing. The final score read: Longford United, 3 goals; Elmwood Cons., nil. ST. BARNABAS' v. HOLLINS GREEN.

The return fixture between these teams was played on Saturday on the Lovely-lane ground. There was a good number of spectators present when Referee Aldred lined up the players. The visitors, having won the toss, decided to Play up the slope, and from the kick off the game was evenly contested, each side attacking in turn. The half-backs were especially promin- ent. As the game proceeded the Saints gradu- ally gained the advantage over their opponents, and shot better when ther got near the goal. Vernon and Houghton were the chief source of danger to the visitors' defence. but Perrin and his backs played a very good game. The visit- ors' forwards made many dangerous raids, but Glover and Long proved capable of dealing with them, and Shaw had not many shots to deal with, whilst at the opposite end the home forwards,
being well supported by their half-back line, lowered the visitors' citadel twice before the interval.

In the second half the game was not so evenly contested, and the visitors did not play up to their reputation. Consequently their goal had to undergo bombardment for the greater portion of this moiety, and had it not been for the good work of Perrin in goal, ably supported by the backs, their citadel would have been captured many times. It was only rarely that dirvisit- ing forwards gave any trouble to the Emile de- fence, and whenever they did Shaw, Glover and Long proved themselves equal to the occasion. The visitors were best represented by their de- fenders, their forwards always appearing to be in difficulties when in front of goal and unable to accept chances. The result was: St. Barna- bas', 4 goals; Hollins Green, nil.

NEWTON CONS. v. EARLESTOWN ST.
JOHN'S MISSION.

The above teams met on Saturday on the ground of the former club, in the first of their League fixtures, and owing to the keen rivalry between the clubs there was a big crowd of spec- tators present when the teams turned out under the control of Referee S. C. Essenhigh, and in the following order:— Newton Cons.: Dagnall ; Lawrance and Tithers ; Atkin, Clark and Porter; Beresford, Jones, Rowbotham, Smart and Gleaves. Mission: Massey; Winders and priffiths.; Tay- lor, X. Eaton and Theobald; Wallas, Jarrett, A. Eaton, Sherlock and Plumpton. The home team had choice of ends and A. Eaton set the ball rolling. The Cons, were quickly put on the defensive, and the -Mission came very near scoring in the first few minutes of the game. After relief had been gained, a free kick against Porter endangered the home goal, but the shot went wide. From the goat kick the Cons. forced the visitors back, and a very easy chance of opening the score was lost by the home forwards. During continued pres- sure Winders and Griffiths defended very stub- ' bornly, and play was transferred to the home quarter, where Dagnall saved when a score seemed certain. A little later a penalty was given against Porter for a back charge. Jarrett took the kick and scored for the Mission. Play now became more keen and a fast pace was set up. The Cons. pressed very hard, but Beresford shot over the bar when in a favourable position. The homesters continued to have the best of the exchanges, but could not pierce the visitors' de- fence, and during a raid on the home goal, two oppq,!ing players collided, and one of them, a Mission boy, had to retire for a short time. Owing to excitement, chances were missed at both ends, and from a strong attack Massey had to concede a corner to clear. F^resford placed theffiag kick well in the goalmo 11, but Massey saved in fino style. The Missio t broke away, and were attacking hotly when Le interval was called with them leading by one goal to nil. The second portion opened with a determined attack on the Mission goal, but Massey proved very safe. Play continued in the visitors' half, and a penalty was given for hands against the defenders. Smart took the kick, but shot over the bar. Mid-field play 'followed, until the Cons, gradually worked into the visitors' quar- ters again, where they failed to take advantage of a well-placed corner kick. The home defence was then called upon, but cleared successfully. The game at this juncture was very even in char- acter, and the ball travelled quickly from end to end. On one occasion Massey was very fortu- nate in saving at the expense of a corner, the kick from which was placed wide. For a time the Mission defence were sorely tried, but the home forwards were not able to take the chances that were offered them. Eventually the Mission forwards, by good combination, set up an attack on the home goal, and when in the act of shoot- ing one of their forwards was pulled down by one of the defenders. Plumpton took the free kick and scored a second goal for the Mission. Good play in mid-field followed, both sets of backs kicking very strongly. A. Eaton scored again for the Mission close upon time. The result was: St. John's Mission, 3 goals; Newton Cons., nil. LATCHFORD BAPTISTS V. FAIRFIELD ATHLETIC.

These teams met on the Weaste-lane ground before a fair crowd. The following • players lined up : Baptists Walker and McGuire; Done, Reyes and Jackson; McDennatt, Rodgers, Pear- son, Vardy and Clarke. Athletic: Beaman: Monks and Johnson; Lea, Roberts and Brooks; Woods, Challinor, Osborne, Short and Bates. The referee was Mr. W. Dennett. The home team won the toss and the visitors, kicking off with a strong breeze behind them, were soon in the vicinity of the home goal, Wyatt being called upon several times to clear. The Baptists, by long passing, transferred play to the visitors' end, and forced a corner kick. This proved fruitless, and the visitors broke away into home territory, where Osborne beat the home backs and baffled Wyatt with a grand shot. Straight from the centre kick the Baptists made a determined attack anon the visitors' goal, and one shot struck the cross-bar. From the rebound Rodgers equalised the score. A few minutes later Short regained the lead for the visitors. From this on to the interval the visitors had the best of the exchanges, and Wyatt was repeatedly called upon to save, but no further goals had been scored when half-time was called with the score: Fairfield, 2 goals; Baptists, 1 goal. On resuming the home team had the assist- ance of the wind, and for some time they en- joyed the best of the game. Clarke was very prominent during this period, and was success- ful in equalising the score. This was the means of infusing 'added energy into the game, and the visitors were more aggressive.. They were awarded a free kick just outside the penalty area. The ,ball struck the cross-bar, and Short, meeting it on the rebound, gave Wyatt no chance. To the end the game was contested very keenly, and the Baptists worked hard to gain
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1914.

div.head: JUNIOR MEDAL COMPETITION POSTPONED.
div.p: JUNIOR MEDAL COMPETITION POSTPONED.

The monthly meeting of the League was held on Wednesday evening at the Red Lion Hotel, Mr. P. Booth presiding, and there being a good attendance of club delegates. The minutes of the previous meeting were read and accepted. Owing to there not being sufficient entries sent in for the Junior Medal Competition it was decided to postpone the competition until February.
A vote of sympathy was passed with Perrins, .of Hollins Green, who was unfortunate enough to get his leg broken in a match against Fairfield Athletic, but is now progressing satisfactorily.

div.head: NOW 111 CHESHIRE LEAGUE. STOCKTON HEATH v. PARTINGTON JUNIORS.
div.p: NOW 111 CHESHIRE LEAGUE. STOCKTON HEATH v. PARTINGTON JUNIORS.

The above teams met on Saturday on the ground of the latter. Partington won the toss, and started with the wind and slope in their favour. From the kick-off the "Heathens" at once became aggressive, and Lloyd gave trouble to Pearson, the home custodian. The visitors continued to press until offside against Vernon sent them back. The home team made progress on their left, but Chesters and Hooper cleared the danger away, and Barlow, the visi- tors' centre-half, passed out to Lloyd, who, beating their opponents, scored with a fast, rising shot, which gave the home goalkeeper no chance. Partington again tried to break through the defence, but, owing to good play by the visitors, they were repulsed, and, during the next ten minutes, the "Heathens" put the ball through twice, but were ruled offside on both occasions. Hazlehurst and Bell, on the home right, maae tracks for the visitors' goal, when the first-named sent in a stinging shot, which Hooper saved at the expense of a corner. The flag-kick was well placed, but Chester I cleared in grand style. From a free-kick the visiting forwards combined well together, and Pearson centring finely. Vernon drove the leather into the net and scored a second goal. Even play followed, but the interval arrived with the score: Stockton Heath, 2 goals; Par- tington Juniors, nil. The home team opened the second portion in spirited fashion and Powell tested Hooper with a long shot, which was easily got away. The home right wing was most prominent, but Pearson shot in erratic fashion, and the ball went wide. The visitors next attacked and the home goalkeeper was called upon by lamb- lett, Vernon and Lloyd in quick succession. Even play in mid-field followed for a while, after which Vernon raced away in the centre and sent in a low shot, which struck the up- right. Pearce met the ball on the rebound and banged it into the net. This reverse roused the home team, who raced to the visitors' end, but finished weakly. The closing stages were much in favour of the visitors, but no further goals were added. Result: Stockton Heath, 3 goals; Partington Juniors, nil.

div.head: HOLLINS GREEN RESERVES v. PADDING-
div.p: HOLLINS GREEN RESERVES v. PADDING-
TON RESERVES.
These teams met at Hollins Green on Satur- day, a well-fought game ending in a victory for the locals by 2 goals to 1 goal.

SANKEY ATHLETIC v. BEAMONT UNITED Sankey Athletic were at home to Beamont United on Saturday, and were, on the whole, very unlucky to lose. Most of the scoring was in the first half, when six goals were put on, Beamont securing four and the Athletic the other two. The final score was: Beamont United, 5 goals; Sankey Athletic, 3. PENKETH ALBION v. SANKEY WHITE

div.head: STAR.
div.p: STAR.

These clubs met at Penketh on Saturday, when the locals, playing dashing football, van- quished the visitors by ten goals to nothing. Nine of the goals came in the second half. The scorers were: L. Jones (4), H. Clark (3), H. Glover (1), H. Pearson (1), and E. Moly- neaux (1). BEWSEY ALBION v. ST. ELPHIN'S C.L.B.

These teams met on the Lovely-lane ground. At the outset the Albion rushed to the visitors' goal, which had a very narrow escape. After repeated attacks the home team were awarded a free-kick, from which F. Sutton scored. The visitors then attacked the home goal, but the defence prevailed. On changing ends the home team again pressed the visitors' goal, but with- out result. The game was more evenly con- tested this half. Near the end A. Hewitt, on receiving, passed inside to R. White, who, after eluding the visitors' backs, scored. The home team ran out victors by 2 goals to nil.
PADGATE v. DARESBURY.

This match was played at Padgate on Satur- day. The visitors won the toss and took advan- tage of the wind. Daresbury were the first to attack, but found the home defence too strong. Padgate came near to scoring, Houghton grazing the post with a good shot. S. Hardman and Hig- ginson combined and the latter opened the score. Padgate pressed and the visitors' full-back put the ball through his own goal. The visitors strove hard to get level, but without result. Padgate took up the attack and from a centre from the right wing, Higginson headed through. Half:time arrived with the score: Padgate, 3 goals; Daresbury, nil. On resuming the visitors became more aggres- sive and Foster opened their score. This put life into them. From a melee in the goalmouth the home full-back put the ball through. The homesters endeavoured to add to their score, and the visitors' goalkeeper was called upon to save time after time. The visitors broke away and Adams put the scores level. Play then became most exciting, each side striving for the lead. Near the close the homesters made a raid on the visitors' goal, and Williamson, receiving, scored with a fast rising shot. His was undoubtedly the best goal of the match. Result: Padgate, 4 goals; Daresbury, 3 goals.
