div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

An Amalgamation.—At a meeting of the War- rington Board of Guardians on Wednesday it was reported that sanction had been obtained for the amalgamation of the Winwick and Rixton sub-districts for registration purposes.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

Church Anniversary.--Saturday was the sixth anniversary of the consecration of the Church of St. Margaret and All Hallows, and a special commemoratary service was held on Sunday evening. Appropriate music was rendered by the choir, including the anthems "We bow in prayer" and "The radiant morn," while the "Magnificat" and "Nun; Dimittis" were sung to Dr. Burnett's setting. The preacher was the Vicar (the Rev. G. Vale-Owen), who took for his text St. John xiv. 1, 2 and 3: "If ye believe in God, ye believe in Me. In My Father's house are many mansions; if it were not so I would have told you. Igo to prepare a place for you."

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

Civil Guard to Undertake Patrol Duty.—The members of the Moore and District Civil Guard assembled for drill in the Riding School at Wal- ton Hall on Saturday evening. They went through various evolutions under the able direc-

tion of Sergt. Jones.—At the conclusion of their work the members were addressed by their Commandant (Mr. H. L. Wynne Jones), who commended to them the suggestion of the Chief Constable of Cheshire that they should do nightly patrol duty, the object of the patrols being to reinforce the existing guard at Moore- lane Swing Bridge, the L. and N.-W. Railway Viaduct, Walton Arches, and the Stag Swing Bridge at Walton Inferior.—The whole of the seventy men present offered themselves for such duty.—The following township leaders paraded with the men :—Acton Grange and Walton Superior: Leader, Sir Gilbert Greenall; deputy- leader, Mr. Nicholas Birchall. Daresbury : Leader, Mr. John Wright; deputy-leader, Mr. J. H. Ravenscroft. Hatton: Leader, Mr. Tohn J. Whitley. Moore: Leader, Mr. C. Gough; deputy-leader, Mr. Stephen Plimpton. Lower Walton: Leader, Mr. Alfred Banks; deputy- leader, Mr. Walter Leech.
Our Stock of Overcoats is fully mobilised in all
Departments.

div.head: CALAIS-NOT YET. I NAVY ___ r CO-OPERATES.
div.p: CALAIS-NOT YET. I NAVY ___ r CO-OPERATES.
GREATEST GERMAN EFFORT FAILS

The Germans having failed to reach Paris or Warsaw turned with great viciousness upon Calais and professed that it was the key not to Paris, but to En-gland. How great was the importance attached to this enterprise by the Germans is seen by the fact that the German Emperor ordered his troops to take Ypres at all costs. He came in person to the firing line to see them do it. Huge reinforcements were poured into S.-W. Belgium, but the Allies poured in men, too, and the reports were uniform records of ground held and slight progress made, thanks to the devotion and doggedness of the French, British and Belgian troops, and the help the Fleet were able to give on the coast.

div.head: BELGIAN ARMY.
div.p: THE BELGIAN ARMY.

Fighting on the last remaining fringe of their country, the Belgians have fought with the bravery and success that have marked them out for the highest praise since the war began. One would think they could do no more, says a correspondent, and yet they fight on, and find the courage and energy even to charge. When Antwerp fell the Belgian Army was given the task of holding the lines of Yser for 48 hours as a stop-gap till reinforcements arrived. It was eight days before any came, and even now, after a fortnight of the most terrible fighting in the war, it is still the Belgians who are bearing the brunt of the German attacks. At the beginning of the war the Belgian Army numbered something over 90,000 men. After the fall of Antwerp its effectives were reduced to about 40,000. In the last fortnight they must have lost at least a third of that number.

div.head: TERRITORIALS DISTINGUISH
div.p: TERRITORIALS DISTINGUISH
THEMSELVES.
London Scottish Make Bayonet Charge

The London Scottish, the first British Terri- torial Regiment to go into action, covered them- selves with glory on Saturday. The London Scottish took an important part in the action, says the "Times" correspondent. They fought well and gloriously. They gave for their country all that they could give. The order came that they were to move out to Ypres. They were transported in motor vehicles. Gladly they went, glad to be at last in the forefront of the battle. Here, as I informed you yesterday, the enemy had renewed- their attempt to break through our lines. They were in great force, strong in .artillery. At Hollebecko and at Messines, between Ypres and Warneton, our lines were hard pressed. The Territorials went to support the Cavalry Brigade holding the trenches there. They were formed up under the crest of a hill. They advanced over the hillcrest right into the battle line. Down the slope they went, over heavy ground and beet crops, coming at once under a fierce artillery fire.

On they went into an inferno of shot and shell. They advanced in short rushes. Many fell. In such a hell it seemed impossible that any of them could live. The battalion did not falter. On they went to the enemy's trenches. Then the enemy came at them in overwhelming numbers, with bayonets fixed. It was an awful moment.

The London Scottish fixed bayonets, too. They did not wait for the attack. They charged the advancing enemy. The impact was terri- fic. Overborne by numbers our men recoiled. Our men re-formed and charged again, again, and again. And then the German infantry turned and ran. The day was won.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL BELGIAN ARTILLERY.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL BELGIAN ARTILLERY.

The Belgian Press Bureau on Sunday issued the following con.munication : Two Belgian batteries, comprising eight pieces of artillery, have fired 8,000 rounds on the Yser in eight days. The Belgian shells destroyed most of the German batteries which were un- masked. MANY GERMAN PRISONERS.

According to statistics furnished by our ser- vice in the rear, the French reported on Sun- day, during the week from the 14th to the 20th alone there were interned 7,683 German pri- soners. These figures do not include wounded under the care of our ambulance corps nor detachments en route from front to rear.

div.head: BRITISII SOLDIERS TRANSFERRED TO BELGIUM. – Heavy German Losses.
div.p: BRITISII SOLDIERS TRANSFERRED TO BELGIUM. - Heavy German Losses.

The British Force, including the Indian con- tingent, has been transferred from the Aisne to the Belgian frontier and has helped to meet the great German onslaught to get to Calais. A dispatch from an " Eye-witness Present with General Headquarters" describes the fighting in which the British troops were engaged from October 20th to 25th. Constant attacks on our

positions were made by the Germans with des- perate bravery. The defenders held their fire until the last moment and then swept away the enemy's solid masses. On October 21st the German losses south-east of Armentieres alone are estimated at 6,000. That night the 104th Regiment left 400 dead in the British lines, while 300 others fell under artillery fire further out. During the 22nd and 23rd the German losses were again extremely heavy. In one quarter the British picked up 1,500 dead, all killed on the 23rd. The six days' fighting ended with the British advancing once more.

div.head: KAISER'S EVIL INFLUENCE.
div.p: KAISER'S EVIL INFLUENCE.

The Kaiser's presence in any part of the field seems to be of ill-omen for his troops, says the "Times." What happened before Nancy and Warsaw has now happened also near Ypres. On Monday it was announced that the Kaiser was with the troops in front of Ypres. On Tuesday the French official communique noted that south of Dixmude and in the direction of Gheluvelt the Allies had made a marked ad- vance.

div.head: "PRODIGIOUS SLAUGIITER " OF
div.p: "PRODIGIOUS SLAUGIITER " OF
THE ENEMY.

The "Eye-witness present with our Head- quarters" in the field describing the attacks of the Germans on the British lines between Octo- ber 26 and 30, says this is "the most bitterly contested battle which has been fought in the western theatre of war." The centre of this battle has been in the neighbourhood of Ypres. Violent assaults were made by the enemy, who in their repulses lost whole columns. "Pro- digious slaughter" was done by the British ar- tillery, and two German Bin. howitzers were destroyed by gun fire. Despite considerable loss the British consistently held, their own. An unbroken line has been maintained and the Allied position strengthened, and reinforce- ments of every kind have been sent to meet the attacks now threatened. Indian troops are in the fighting line. The enemy have abandoned in retreat, pris- oners, wounded', a large quantity of material, and guns engulfed in the inundation caused when the sluices were opened by the Belgian Army. At many points the offensive seems to have passed again to the Allies. They have evidently repeated their tactics of waiting for the succes- sive waves of the German advance to break against their resistance.

div.head: BATTLESHIP'S BIG GUNS AGAIN
div.p: BATTLESHIP'S BIG GUNS AGAIN
IN ACTION.

The Press Bureau issued the following on Saturday night:— The Venerable (Captain V. H. G. Bernard) has been in action again all day in support of the Belgian left, aided by the gunboats and flotillas. This is now the fourteenth day of the naval bombardment.

The Venerable is a battleship of 15,000 tons, carrying four 12in. guns. BRITISH CRUISER SUNK BY SUBMARINE. H.M.S. Hermes, a protected second-class cruiser, completed for sea in 1900, was torpedoed and sunk by a German submarine in the Straits of Dover on Saturday.

The Hermes was sister to the Highflyer, and carried a complement of 450 men. Nearly all the men were saved by destroyers, the latest list giving the casualties as three dead, three severely wounded, four slightly wounded and nineteen missing. Recently the Hermes had been used as a sea- plane-carrying ship, and several of those missing were connected with the naval air service.

div.head: _•. GERMAN SQUADRON OFF THE
div.p: _•. GERMAN SQUADRON OFF THE
COAST.

The Admiralty announced on Tuesday night that early that morning an enemy squadron fired .on the Halcyon, a coastguard gungoat engaged in patrolling, wounding one of her crew. The Halcyon having reported the presence of the enemy ships, "various naval movements were made." They retreated hastily, "shadowed by light cruisers," which failed to bring them to action before dusk. The rearmost German cruiser, in retirement, threw out a number of mines and submarine D 5 was sunk by exploding one of these. Two officers and two men who were on the bridge of the sub- marine, which was running on the surface, were saved.
Nothing else happened during the day in home waters, except that the gunboat flotilla had been available in support of the Belgian left flank.

div.head: GERMAN CRUISER SUNK.
div.p: GERMAN CRUISER SUNK.

The German cruiser Yorck has been sunk off the German coast. Berlin reports attribute the loss of the Yorck to her striking a chain of mines. Over half the crew are said to have been saved; of the other men, 250 in number, there is no news. From the known facts it appears likely that the Yorck met with disaster when returning from the raid across the North Sea made by the enemy on Tuesday. When war began the Germans had nine armoured cruisers, two of them old ships. Now the Yorck has gone, and the Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, im- proved Yorcks, are not available for European service. The lost cruiser was of the same size, but was newer and more powerfully armed than, the Monmouth.

div.head: ON THE AISNE FRONT.
div.p: ON THE AISNE FRONT.
DIVERTING ATTENTION.

Last week-end a reference to Verdun was made in the Berlin Wireless Circular, which implied that the Allied right, or eastern wing, was about to be crushed in a decisive battle. After all the boasts about Calais this attempt to direct German public attention another way was significant. RENEWED ACTIVITY ON THE AISNE.

Paris on Monday reported assaults by The inemy made in several places along the Aisne. Above Vailly, on the heights Chemin-des- Dames, in the region of Reims, between the Argonne and the Meuse, and on the heights of the Meuse, the Allied line had been tested by day or by night with infantry or with heavy guns. In every case it had stood the test.

..,... - Elsewhere it had crept fo--1;;;;:d7 Ties; slight 1 advances were recorded in th direction of Tmcy-le-Val and in certain pa i's of the right bank of the Aisne, between the oret de l'Aigle and Soissons.

On the line of the Aisne it was reported on Wednesday there had again been a good deal of fighting, with a slight retirement of the Allies at one point, compensated by progress east of the Foret de l'Aigle. Between the Oise and the Moselle he delivered on Wednesday assaults at various places along the entrenched front. All these assaults have finally failed. The Allies were holding their own on Wednes- day everywhere from the Belgian coast to the Vosges.

div.head: RUSSIA ADVANCES
div.p: RUSSIA ADVANCES
TERRIBLE LOSSES OF TIIE GERMANS.

On Sunday afternoon the Russian headquar- ter staff issued a statement, saying:— On the East Prussian frontier our troops have progressed in the region of Vladislavow, in the forest of Rominten. The attacks made by the Germans in the Bakalarzewo region yesterday have ceased owing to the terrible losses suffered by the enemy. On the other side of the Vistula we are ad- vancing victoriously along the whole front. We have occupied Piotrkow, Opoceno, and Ozarow. Fighting took place on the roads leading to Opaboff, where we routed the enemy's rear- guard and took 400 prisoners, quick-firing guns, and convoys of provisions. AUSTRIANS DRIVEN OFF. -

On the River San, near Lezachovo, a Russian regiment, entrenching itself step by step, reached the enemy's positions, and, profiting by a panic among the Austrians, took by storm a fortified position. We there took five officers and 500 soldiers prisoners, and also captured some quick-firing guns.

- A detachment of the enemy which descended the Carpathians and entrenched itself near Nad- vorna was attacked and driven off. Berlin, which had been inclined to make much of certain preliminary advances, said the fight- ing was " proceeding without result," a form of words used several days earlier about the War- saw defeat.

SUCCESS ON PRUSSIAN FRONTIER. The Russian Headquarter Staff of the Com- mander-in-Chief issued the following communi- cation on Tuesday On the East Prussian front the Germans are now everywhere acting on the defensive. Our troops have advanced in some districts and have any captured two guns, a searchlight, and prisoners. Beyond the Vistula, in the region north-west of the Pilitca, our troops, advancing without 7 Lsidak esra,balnedeßngoazgpermzae.nts, have occupied Snzayde considerable,

AUSTRIANS REPULSED. On the Eadoszyice-Kielce front the enemy is retiring in the direction of Wtoszczowa- Fur- ther to the north-east of Kielce the Austrians attempted a more obstinate resistance, but were repulsed and lost three cannon, five mitrailleuses and 1,500 prisoners. They only hold their posi- tions on the lower course of the river Opatowka. On the lower course of the San our troops con- tinue to cross to the left bank of the river, and have taken the village of Make and part of the frontier position further north of Rozwadow,

capturing two cannon and mitrailleuses. In the Nisko region a desperate battle continues. We have taken 250 prisoners. On November 3 the Russians gained a decisive success over the Austrians along the whole front Kielce-Sandomlerz. The enemy fell hurriedly back and we occupied Sandomierz, an import- ant strategical point. In the region south of Kielce within the last week the Russians had taken 200 officers and 16,000 men prisoners and have captured several dozen guns and machine guns.

GERMAN RETREAT IN EAST PRUSSIA. Petrograd, Nov. 5. The following official communique from the Great Army Headquarters is published here to- day:— We continue to progress on the East Prussian front. The Germans are falling back along the whole front, only keeping a fortified position in the region of Wergboliwo (? Wirballen). On the left bank of the Vistula the Russian Army is continuing its vigorous offensive, pur- suing the retreating enemy. The crossing of the San by bur troops continues with success. The Austrians are retreating.
GREAT VICTORY BY RUSSIANS.
Austrians Routed in Galicia.

• llordeaux, Friday. At a Cabinet meeting to-day. M. Delcasse read a telegram announcing that the Russian Army had achieved a complete victory, and that the Austrians had been routed on the entire front in Galicia.
SOUTH AFRICA.
REBELLION GROWS WEAKER AND WEAKER.

Early in the week it was reported that the South African rebellion was in a poor way. In the western area an additional 50 of Maritz's rebels had been captured. Colonel Alberts, commanding a Union force, defeated General Beyers's followers in the Lichtenburg district, killing 13, wounding 30, and taking 240 prisoners. Lichtenburg is in the Western Transvaal, about 130 miles west- south-west of Hustenburg, whence General Botha set out to attack the rebels the day after their rising was announced. Beyers, himself a fugitive from justice, seems to have been as little of a success as a traitor es his friend Maritz, whose few remaining men grow continually fewer. Only De Wet remained to bo dealt with, and he, it is known, is ill-equipped for a struggle. The Governor-General of the Union of South Africa reports that Colonel Brits on Tuesday, October 27th, sent a patrol of 50 men in the direction of Schuitsdrift, where they encoun- tered 150 of Maritz's men. The patrol cap- tured eight of Maritz's men, including two lieutenants. diaritz lost several killed and wounded. There were no losses on our side. Captain Beukes, Lieutenant Furter, and 58 men of the Active Citizen Force raised in Namaqualand, surrendered voluntarily to Com- mandant Studer and were brought in by him to Springbok. It is understood that Maritz's following has split up into small bands, varying in numbers, which are roaming aimlessly in proximity to the German border. Three men who surren- dered from a party of 60 under Lieutenant Joubert, who has been wounded, state that lie instructed then' to disperse and make for their homes.

div.head: TURKEY IN TWO MINDS. ATTACKS AND SAYS THE GERMANS DID IT.
div.p: TURKEY IN TWO MINDS. ATTACKS AND SAYS THE GERMANS DID IT.

Following the acts of war in the Black Sea by Turkey, without having made a declaration of war, there has been quite a Turkish-liko per- formance in the art of shuffling. On Sunday the Foreign Office issued a com- munication dealing with the interpretation which the Sublime Porte placed upon the neu- trality which it had affected to profess towards the Powers of the Triple Entente since the beginning of the war, and with the British diplomatic representations to Turkey upon this subject. Great Britain and her Allies have, it is proved, been exceedingly patient in the face of constant and deliberate provocations offered by the Porte at the instigation of Germany. Agents have been sent to preach hatred and hostility to Great Britain throughout Syria, Egypt and India, whilst hostilities against Russia and an invasion of Egypt has been begun. The British Government therefore considered it necessary to take whatever action may be required to protect British interests, British territory, and also Egypt, from attack. Among the steps taken by Turkey are the tending of troops through Palestine for an in- vasion of Egypt, the making of strategic roads and the preparation of mines for laying in the Gulf of Akaba. As the Foreign Office statement says: "Vigorously assisted by the Ambassadors of Germany and Austria, the German military elements in Constantinope have been persist- ently doing their utmost to force Turkey into war, both by their activities in the service of the Turks and by the bribes of which they have been so lavish." BLAMING GERMANY. Still, Turkey did no declare war, and some of her officials represented that she desired peace. Reports reached London on Monday that the drand Vizier had disavowed hostile intentions and placed the responsibility for the bombardment of Russian ports upon the Ger- mans in Turkey. Meanwhile, the Turkish Ambassador remained in London. He was busy negotiating with the Foreign Office, and an apology was said to have been tendered to the Allies. AKABA BOMBARDED.

A British cruiser, the Minerva, -has shelled the Turkish town of Akaba, and a landing party has destroyed the fort, the barracks, the shops, and the Post Office. The Turks suffered some losses before they evacuated the town. Apparently they had with them a German officer. Akaba stands near the southern end of the Turco-Egyptian frontier, and there is reason to believe that the Ottoman generals in- tended, and may still intend, to advance from the town against the Suez Canal.
BOMBARDMENT OF DARDANELLES. A combined British and French squadron bom- barded the Dardanelles forts at. long range at daybreak on November 3.

The forts replied, but no ships were hit and the Allies suffered no loss, only one projectile falling alongside. The material damage to the forts cannot he estimated, but a large explosion, accompanied by dense volumes of black smoke, occurred at Holies Fort.

INDIA AND EGYPT. It is not expected that the action of Turkey will in any way affect the loyalty of India or Egypt, in which places the Germans hoped to create strife. The Aga Khan has issued an elo- quent manifesto to his fellow subjects in India condemning the aggression of Turkey. TERRITORIALS IN EGYPT. In Cairo a review has been held of the British Territorials stationed there. The troops, who formed a stronger force of all arms than any other seen in Egypt for many years, were obvi- ously in splendid condition.

div.head: ENGLAND DECLARES WAR ON
div.p: ENGLAND DECLARES WAR ON
TURKEY.

Great Britain has formally declared war on Turkey and formally annexed the island of Cyprus. The Turkish Ambassador left Lon- don on Thursday afternoon. British warships bombarded the Dardanelles entrance.
On the Armenian frontier Russian troops are acting with vigour. They have assailed Turk- ish forces in several places, driven them from their positions, and inflicted considerable losses on them.
Cyprus lies only forty miles from the Syrian
coast and would provide an excellent base for operations against Turkey in Asia. • -int The Armenians are greatly excited, belieco the liberation of theiP country from 111.1."1 misrule to be at hand.

A lemon from which most of the •' ...,i juice has been squeezed does just as well as a freshly-cut lemon. Rinse the article in clean hot water afterwards. Then dry and polish , - with a clean soft cloth. Very few people make good short-bread. It .1 seems it does not matter how good your recipe may be, it is essential that the oven door re- ceives especial attention. After you put the , short-bread into the oven, leave the door ajar for ten minutes, then close it gently and cook 1 , , for twenty minutes to half an hour. , H The Care of Leather Furniture. PI Leather furniture is often allowed to lose its 10 brightness and beauty because housekeepers seem to think that it requires nothing more I k than the duster to keep it in good condition. But this is a mistake. Leather needs constant care to prevent its becoming too dry and being 'readily liable to tear. In the first place, a little soap iii.d water ?nos be applied to wash off the dust and soil—just a very little soapy water, applied in the folds sled crevices of the leather with a paint-brush. The 1\ I lather will darken the leather but only tempo- rarily, and the leather must be rubbed dry afterwards. When it is dry it is advisable to use some . , 1 good, prepared oil, or a home-made combination 5 ' of sweet oil and vaseline, rubbed well into the leather, which must afterwards be polished dry with a cloth. . , 3 If leather is nourished thus three or four 4 times a year, it will retain its gloss, beauty and elasticity, and will keep a gocd colour.

HERE AND THERE. A widow always talks about how young she was when she first.married. War News in the Kitchen. Mary Jane (at the climax of fearful story of German spy) : "And when the police searched the cellars they found enough ambition to blow up the whole of London."—"Punch." Every Reason to be Sure. Arthur: Are you sure she loves you? Jack: Yes. When I told her I had no money to marry on, she asked me if I couldn't borrow some. Notice in a Battersea Window. "Bride Cakes. Any Size. To Suit All Pockets." In these days of narrow skirts most women will find the guinea_ size sufficient.—" Punch." American Envy. "We just had a letter from my daughter, the countess," said the proud mother. "Is that so? How much money does she want this time?" sneered the neighbour, whose daugh- ter had married a Mere banker. How She Succeeded. "Now you've achieved something !" he ex- claimed. "These are exactly like the cakes mother used to make. How did you do it?" "I'll give you the recipe," replied the wife, "I used margarine instead of butter, eggs a week old, I put alum in the flour, and added plenty of water to the milk." A Trifle Frosty. "Sir," said the young man, as he entered the library for the purpose of interviewing the father of the only girl, "I am in love with your daughter. Have you any objection to my suit?" The old man looked the young man over from head to foot. "I sure have," he replied. "Why, I wouldn't wear a misfit suit like that to a dog fight. Why don't you try some other tailor?"
